div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

SOME men have greatness thrust upon them, but they think they achieved it. HAPPI:TESS consists largely in forgetting the things you can't have. THE surest thing about first love is that it is not likely to be the last. HE "I always keep my word." She "Won't anybody take it?" Baowx : "She asked me to call again." Jones: "Hasn't she any other friends?" THE OLD STORY.—" You are beside yourself." She: "Seeing double again, are you?" Nothing pleases a man so much as to be coaxed to do a thing he wants to do, anyway. ONCE, AT LEAST.—" Women are seldom good listeners." "Unless you are making a proposal." Tact is being able to tell a lie without letting the listener know you know he knows you are not telling the truth. "I wonder what got Bluebeard starting to cut off his wives' heads?" " Very likely the idea occurred to him while he was at the theatre behind a big hat." ARTHUR: "I woull marry that girl but for one thing." Chester: "Afraid to pop the question ?" Arthur: "No. Afraid to question her pop." WHAT DID SHE MEAN ?—He: "I see it aIL You love another." She: "Well, you're another." A LITERARY QUERY.—Bride: "What is most needed by the poet of to-day?" Skalde "Postage stamps." His DESIRE.—OId Flint (savagely): "So you want to become my son-in-law, young man?" Young Swift (promptly) : "No ; I merely want to marry your daughter." AT TILE MENAGERIE.—First street arab : "I heard tell that camels often has to go a week with- out a drink." Second street arab : No wonder they get their backs up." REASON ENOUGH. Packer: "That sailors' chorus was awful ! What was the matter?" Stage manager: "The tars couldn't get the right pitch." TOMMY (to ycung man visiting Tommy's sister): "I've got a lot of money in my bank." Mr. Freshman : " Indeed ? Where did you get it all ? " Tommy : "Every time Maud gets a new sweet- heart he gives me some pennies to stay out of the room."

CITY MAN—" I should think you would find life very dreary," Villager? " He:al 7 "I just tell you this is a pretty lively plaae for its size." "I should not suppose from the looks of things any- thing ever happened here." "That's where you're mistaken. Why, it ain't two weeks since we had an eclipse of the moon." "I am really delighted at the interest my boy Tommy is taking in his writing," said Mrs. Hickleby. "He spends two hours a day at it." "Really? How strange I How did you get him to do it?" "Oh, as for that, I told him to write me out a list of everything he wanted for Christ- mas, and he's still at it."

" Excasz me, Mrs. Hiredum, but your servant seems very familiar." "Yes, I know; but she has been so long in the family that we overlook many 'things. Indeed, we regard her much as the Eng. fish do an old retainer." "That is different, of course. One puts up with many things from an -old and tried servant. How long has she been with you ? " "Seven weeks yesterday."

THE Basr WHEATEN BREAD.—" Dick" Martin was known throughout Ireland as a most benevo- lent but eccentric character. When in the Irish Parliament, he seconded a motion for an inquiry into the causes of the adulteration of flour. After giving some odd reasons for the necessity of an inquiry, he exclaimed, with vehemence: "As to bread, Mr. Speaker, why, the beat wheaten bread we have in the county of Galway is that made from potatoes and oatmeal 1" _

Too MANY SYLLABLES. A well-dressed man entered a florist's shop the other day, threw down a large silver coin, and said he wanted some flowers to take home. He was quite unsteady, and the flowers were apparently intended as a domestic peace offering. The florist picked out a dozen chrysanthemums, and the call-r started to leave. At the door he hesitated. "Say," he said, thickly, " whatsh these flowersh, anyway ? " "Chrysanthemums." The customer shook his head. " Gotter have something easier," he said. "Gimme a dozen pinks." BROKE A BRIDE'S HEART.—There is a bitter coolness right in the bosom of a family I know, and it happened in this wise: They haven't been married very long, and she is in just that stage of devotion when she wants to do everything for him. The band about his hat needed renewing the other day, and thinking to surprise him, she put a brand-new ribbon on one day while he was down town. When he came home he noticed the new band. "Who did that?" he asked. " had it done," replied she, coyly. "Well," he snorted, "what born idiot ever put a bow on the wrong side of the hat?" And of course her tender heart was broken, for it isn't given to any woman to understand why self-respect will not allow a man to wear either a hat—bow, or nosegay on his right side.

A WEsrmitix FENCE.—" You say you had that land all fenced before the defendant settled on it?" An attorney in a Government land case was nross-examining a homesteader. "Yes, I did." "Was that fence horse proof?" " Yes ;it was." " Was it bull close?" "Yes." "And pig tight?" "Yes." "What was it made of?" " Well—er— I can't say." I noticed that witness hesitated, floundered for the first time, and the attorney observed it, too. " Was it a rail fence?" "No." "Brush fence ?" "No." "Picket fence ? " "No." " Board fence?" "No." " Wire fence? "No; I don't know what it was made of; but it kept everything out," declared the witness, who had become desperate. "Toll me what that fence was," persisted the attorney. "Well, it was a man with a shot gun." BY the light of his dark lantern the burglar read the following inscription on a card tacked to the outside of the window he was about to pry up with a jemmy: "To All Midnight Callers.—Do not ruin the fastenings of this window by prying it up. The rear door oi the house is always unlocked." "This card is dusty and covered with cob-webs," he said to himself, "It has been here a long time, but I'll just go round and see if that door's still unlocked. If they'd rather have me go in that way, I think I'll humour them." Whereupon he stole softly round to the rear door, opened it, and a man in one of the sleeping-rooms upstairs, awakened by a burglar alarm, came down and shot at him. This inci.-lent shows, dear children, that it is possible to be too confiding. THEY WERE GOOD BOOKS.—" That was a book agent who just went out?" remarked tha man at the next desk, interrogatively. "Yes, it was ; and while I don't usually deal with book agents, I ordered his book." "What was it ?" "It was in ten volunvis' beautifully printed on hand-made, paper, with dekle edges." " Yes, but what was it ?" " Three dollars a volume, and you only have to pay three dollars down, and you get all the book, at once. It was morocco bound, with plares, arid One of the finest specimens of in ill, " Yes, but what VMS the name of the ho !" "It MO ten books, in ten voietnes, I ;..4.1 y.,ti." " Yes, but by whom? Thm'r, you iiiiiierstand ?" A pause. ' Well, I dec,are, I have frog ,tten the name of the author. It was a set et efiiiorbaily's works. But they were beautiful brr.lcs, let me tell von. Why the mischief -should you laugh ?

HOW IT STARTED. —Pinkey : "How lovely I I see you have one of thee splendid new Nonesuch bikes." Ethel " lea; isn't it a dear? What make do you ride?" Pinkley : "I ride a Scorehem." Ethel: "They're magnificent." Pinkley : "Yes en light and durable." Ethel: "How much does your machine weigh?" Pinkley: Twenty.two pounds." Ethel: "Twenty-two pounds! Why, mine only weighs twenty-one." Pinkley : "But then yours, you know, is not so durable. ' Ethel; "The Nonesuch not durable? Why, it is admired by every one." Pinkley : "Nonsense 1 A friend of mine brought one, and it went to pieces in a month." Ethel: "I don't believe it."' Pinkley : "What I You don't believe me?" Ethel: "No I don't. One Nonesuch will outlast a dozen Scorchems. They're the worst. looking rattletraps I ever laid eyes on." Pinkey : (furiously): You're a horrid, contemptible thin,, and I hope you will never speak to nu) again r" Ethel (complacently): "Don't worry. I wouldn-t compromise myself by speaking to anyone who rode a Scorchens.

"WOMEN'S CHAT." Zee Queen and several members of the Royal Family are spending Easter abroad, According to present ar- rangements Her Majesty is to return from the Riviera at the end• of the month, and the Prince of Wales who intended to be at Sandringham for Easter, has altered 'is plans and is remaining on the Continent. This year, se family of the Prince of Wales has been almost as widely scattered as it could be. The Duke of York has been fishing on Deeside, while the Duchess ha been staying in the South of France. The Prince of Wales has also been passing the time by the Mediterranean, while the Princess has gone to Denmark,and the Princess Victoria of Wales is staying at Cromer, that popular resort which Is becoming more and more favoured by Royalty. The Duke of York has jest been presented with a model of IL ALS, Bacchante, in which he and his brother the late Duke of Claienee, made a voyage round the world. The old Baecbante was sold out of the Navy last year, but before being broken up the Shipbuilding Com- pany wrote to the Duke suggesting that he might like a souvenir of the ship in which he passed three years of his youth. His Royal Highness replied that he would be extremely pleased to receive some memento, and it was decided to make a model of the ship's stern out of a portion of her own timbers. The work-has been beauti- fully done, and it was presented to the Duke of York the other day, with a suitalle inscription commemorative of His Royal Elighness'a tour round the world in the years 1879-1882. Very great have been the recent strides in church embroidery, and numerous are the women who have devoted their leisure during the past lent to working A stele, buree, veil, or some other valuable addition to their particular church. The foundation of most of teese is white silk damask, or green silk, sometimes reseiltb an elegant floral scroll worked upon it. Apropos of churches, some sixteen years aeel the church of St. Mary the Virgin, in New York, Mean employing women as soloists, having the bee for chorus work only. The former were not vested, but, wearing a blue veil upon their heads, were pnced, not cons eictiouely,back of the chancel arch. The pnovation was followed by other churches, and proved A complete success. This may be termed the comrneleetnent of the movement in America for the restoratior c•f women to a place in the musical service of the chincb,although it is said that the earliest chorus of vested women were Melbourne. heara at Birmingham, and in Australia at To the value of choral training in cherch music, all great artists alike bear testimony. "Tbe church choirs in America," says Madame Belle Cole, ".are admirable training grounds for the artist, the diecipline exercised over the vo,ce in singing all kinds of eecree music before large congregations being most valuable." Accordieg to Mr. Ed ward Lleyd, it affords excellent grounding in the work of old English composers. ."Young singers," he has said, " spend years studying In Italy, but there they learn only light and operable music. If the heavy music is well mastered the rest pallid be comparatively easy. Madame Belle Cole, like most American women,has all the characteristics of the American woman, being filled with brightness and animatioa from the top of her head which is crowned with a weelth of brown hair, dressed in the latest graceful Parisien style, the waves hanging loosely over the tips of her ears,down to her well-formed well-shod feet. She is of tnedium height, most genial in appearance. Like most women who have made a mark in any special line,this popular singer leads an extremely busy life. Part of each morning is taken up with at- tending to her nouseleo/d matters, ane the remainder is spent in correspondence. Then when the correspondence is over an accompenist works with Madame Cole from one to four o'elock, when comes the daily drive. The songstress herself is a notable Jehu and band es the ribbon with a firm and light touch. Madame Cole holds tilos a singer eheuld never accompany herself. The piano should be a secondary consideration and the thoughts and attention of the vocalist should never be hampered by the care and study which is necessary in order to accompany well. Strapped seams are again decorating many of the newest coats, velvet strappings being mostly employed, often outlined by fine cord, and a neat design in fine braiding. The button and the buckle are other decora- tive influences at work on the coat of the moment, of which those in turquoise and steel are the most popular. Good buttons, by the way, ate a capital investment, for they may be used over and over again. Many society women now-a-days have a collection of buttons, and add a set to r ach gown themselves, selecting " the very button " with the greatest consideration for the cos- tume. Although the wig(' among us makes rule of postponing the choice of a new spring toilette until the end of the present month, few can resist the temptation to indulge in a new hat or toque at this particular season of the year. And we can scarcely marvel that this sbould be so, when we have before us an array of some of the most fascinating specimens contained its the millinery market this Easter. In the matter of trimmings noth- ing stands bolt upright. Everything is softly curved. Quills continue to curl over, in great broad soft ends, as if they were making a perpetual obeisance. They slant moreover, in any way that best suits the angle of the headgear. The art of wood-carving is one that is followed alike by men and women, but women would seem to show the greatest aptitude, and they often combine needle- work with carving, especially in dark oak overmantles, Into which they introduce suitable panels of embroidery. Even the spinning-wheel chair, however elaborately carved, can be greatly improved by a strip of embroi- dery down the back, while many footstools have cared wooden frames, enclosing embroidered velvet. Photo- graph frames may be carved but have an interior mount of satin embroidered with silks and paillettes—a treat- ment which also adds to the beauty of the stamped leather frames. To old ladies, the new giant work comes as a boon and a blessing. It is simply large cross-stitches worked on a closely-woven cotton basket canvas, in the quaint colorings of fifty years no. They could also easily manage the new serge work in which large designs are carried out with long loops, held down by a smaller stitch at the point. The stems are either rope-stitch, or thick wool laid on the fabric and sewn with silk. This has a great effect. Considerable public interest leas arisen in London on the question of smoking upon omnibuses and tramways. A company has been formed to provide penny-in-the-slot machines for the supple of cigarettes on the top of these vehicles, and apparently the omnibus and train con- palsies are quite prepared to give facilities for this pur- pose. There is however, no need for increasing facili- ties for the indulgence of a habit which has already leached dimensions very distastefui to the women and non-smokers who use our public conveyances. It is now hardly possible to venture upon them without serious risk of being temporarily blinded by tobacco ash, se blab is often blown about while still alight, and is liable to damage clothing as well as temper. There is conse- quently an agitation to restrict smoking to all the back benches of the vehicles. In the United States the system is rigidly enforced, and it is about time similar restric- tions were applied in this country with regard to public Conveyances. div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.

hr DEAR NELLIE, There is no season of the year when a woman /eels more inclined to buy new costumes, mantles, and millinery than in the early spring, when the trees are bursting into leaf, and there is a pecaliar and delicious freshness in the air, which seems to make everything that has been worn throughout the winter months seem soiled and shabby, and sut of keeping with the season. This very natural feeling is intensified by the tempting displays of novelties which are displayed on all sides, and nowadays, when really tasteful garments are offered at moderate prices, nearly everyone is able to indulge in at least one new dress and a hat and cape before-the Easter holidays.

A fashionable toque admirably suited for cycling, or to go with a tailor-made gown, can be made of cloth, with the bows edged with narrow jet or silk gimp, or with a tiny ruche formed of bias-cut velvet gathered down at regular intervals. These bows are simply joined up corners of cloth, with a strip of cap-wire running down the centre. Very narrow jet is extremely effective, and the centre finished with a jet buckle. The edge is simple, a bias band, one and a half to two inches deep gathered on, and the curled quills and a couple of velvet rosettes complete the back. A dainty spring hat has a brim of this rainbow cloth in a pretty tone of apple-green, resting on a wreath of prim- roses and ivy; the crown, only a glimpse of which is visible above the folds, is of green-and-cream satin straw, and the aigrette at the side is formed of loops of the rainbow cloth and one of the cream " bottle-brush " plumes which are in fashion this season. These green-and-cream straws are exceed- ingly bright and fresh-looking, and have the advantage of being less conspicuous than the plain green straws.

There are some very smart short-basqued, fitting coats which are to be had at prices to snit' all purses. Very useful models are made of black serge with braiding in fine black and gold braid round basque, revers and cuffs, and a belt of black silk webbing, with clasps of black enamel and gilt.' The &taupe is only some three or four inches deep in most instances, and has just enough fulness to permit it to " set " easily. The sleeves are tight —almost too tight indeed to he comfortable worn over an ordinary dress.aleeve—and very long, the braided cuffs reaching well down over the hand. Many dressy coats have plastrons of white, tan, or biscuit-coloured cloth covered with fine braiding, these fastening invisibly down the front, while the ' collar has tabs to match the plastron, turned out over the high straight neckband. Dark blue cloth trimmed with biscuit cloth, braided in deep blue and silver, has a very smart appearance, worn with a belt of dark blue leather. Narrow strappings of white cloth or kid are seen on other stylish coats, but the contrast is rather too strong to be quite pleasing.
I kas the

The open-fronted coat is a favourite garment for the spring and early summer, and exceedingly useful, as the costume may be varied by different vests or increased in warmth, if desired. The back has oneseam, in the c,..nr re only, and the silk appliqusS designs run up in a point at the centre back. This ccstume is of stone-coloured cloth, faced with a paler stone colour, almost white, and has the applique designs. Braidings can be bought ready to transfer to any garment, or designs in braid and jet, or in Duchesse lace, any of which could be used in similar style. The epaulettes are stiffened and kept fiat, and the collar is also stiffened and wired, and can be turned down or worn high. The coat is held together at the neck by narrow silk cord, fixed to buttons placed just inside the collar. The " three-decker" capes prevail beyond all others and are seen in every shade of cloth. Strap. pings of paler lined cloth trim them in most cases, but not a few have each of their three flounces edged with fine breiding. Both these capes are to be seen in silk velours and cloth, and are genyfally trimmed with full ruches of ribbon as well n with passementerie and braid. Your loving JENNIE.

CHAPTER XXVI. dog days before the second hearing irosecution rushed by with distressing M Mrs. Treheme's estimation. She spent her time in her boudoir bemoaning her Laughter's shattered matrimonial prospects, using to be comforted. Hume came every evening, and had long, st confabulations with Mr. Treherne and doline. After he left, Gvvendoline tried xiably to take a cheerful view of matters, not- _istanding that the dearth of evidence in her ,our remained as great as when the case was first
One day, when Eric had reluctantly admitted that he feared their side would have no witnesses to put forward, she placed her hands on her fi.ther's shoulders and exclaimed, in her bright,

conclusive way: "Of course, it will all come right. There is no doubt I shall be acquitted; and I don't approve of you, dear father, distressing yourself on my account. In a few years' time we shall merely think of the whole episode as a passing cloud that came at a very unfortunate time. lam not going to allow myself to believe that it is possible there can be any other termination to the trial than an acquittal. But very likely the case will not be sent to trial. If it is--"—she stopped, then con- tinued even more gaily—"the moment it is over, and ray innocence proved, I shall ask a certain person, whom I will not mention now--"—she Looked up at her father and laughed—"to give me a big cheque that will cover my expenses for a delightful trip round the world." "You shall have that cheque. I promise it un- conditionally," answered her father, infected with her brightness. "You must come too, or follow me as quickly as you can. What lovely excursions we could go
iogether ! " "Yes ; and I have always had a great wish to travel. But somehow I have put it off from year
to year." "We will not keep to the beaten track, but find out some delightful unexplored place and be captured by brigands and— " Delightful prospect!". interrupted her father,
. - laughing. "But imagine what interesting portraits I could take when we were being detained in the cave for
the ransom."

" Which I trust would not be long. lam afraid, though, that you would not find a single brigand willing to sit for his portrait, unless he intended to appropriate the portrait." "Oh! I forgot. How stupid! Of course, it would lead to his being recognised and captured when he went into the towns. Anyhow, I should have a glimpse into a totally different class of society to what I have been accustomed." "You would certainly have that." Thus it was that Gwendoline Treherne bravely strove to ignore the existence of the trouble-laden clouds that were slowly gathering around her. It was two o'clock on the following Wednesday when the adjourned hearing before the magistrate was opened. Firmly and without flinching she again took her place in the dock, this time appar- ently ignoring the undisguised curiosity with which those assembled in court regarded her. One fact instantly impressed itself on her notice—the court was much more crowded than it had been on the previous occasion, and there were many present whom she had met in society. The first witness called was the server, Thomas Brown, from Messrs. Tuke and Co. He stated that he was well acquainted with the personal appearance of Miss Treherne, she having been from time to time a customer of Messrs. Tuke and Co.'s. He distinctly remembered her calling at the shop on the 15th of July and asking him to cash a cheque which he remembered was signed "Dennis Vane." Asked why it was that the signature had impressed itself so completely on his memory, he said that he had heard Mr. Vane speak at a debating club the night before, and this had led him to particularly notice the signature of the cheque. He had also noticed that the date was written in a different handwriting from the signature —a round unformed hand, he went on to explain. The forged cheque was shown him in court, and he unhesitatingly identified it as the one which Miss Treherne had asked him to cash. Sir Edward Masters here made an effort to shake the witness's testimony, which, unfortunately for the defence, only elicited evidence in favour of the prosecution. He stated that one of his reasons for being absolutely sure of the identity of the accused, was the fact that the dress which she wore on the day, that she called with the cheque, was the same she had worn on one or two previous occasions when he had served her. He was then asked to describe the dress in question, and he did so in a manner which surprised many in court. It appeared that its quaint Algerian trimming had attracted his notice, he having spent several years in Algeria. He had at once recognised that it was of peculiarly fine workmanship. Gwendoline listened most intently to this evi- dence. She knew that the description of the dress exactly tallied with one she had had the previous spring, and ix hich had been referred to in one or two society papers as an example of artistic harmony of colouring. The witness's description of this dress and its trimming was most accurate: the latter had been given to Gwendoline by a cousin, George Melville, on his return from a visit to Algiers. The witness 14 as not only able to give a description of this trimming, but, by reason of his knowledge of colour, supplied the exact names of the harmonising shades of blue which Gwendoline, with true artistic taste, had selected for this costume. The fact that so many people had dilated on its tastefulness rendered this witness's evidence of peculiar weight, and to this she was fully alive. It seemed to her impossible that another dress should exist identically like the one she herself had designed. As the witness emphatically adhered to his state- ments, hope began to die within her. She glanced at her father and saw that he, too, fully recognised the deadly nature of this evidence. Just then Hume turned eagerly to him and asked some ques- tion. But Gwendoline surmised by the manner in which the question was answered that her father did not give the reply which Hume expected. The latter turned away with a look of disappointment, and joined Sir E&ard Masters, who was evidently anxious to have information on some point, on which, however, Eric could not enlighten him. Meanwhile 'Richard Musgrove entered the witness-box. He had taken great pains with his personal appearance, and had succeeded in render- ing himself quiet and respectable-looking to a degree that would have surprised his sister Bella had she been present. But that discreet individual preferred remaining at home on this occasion. Richard Musgrove stated that the accused came to his shop on the 15th of July, and asked him to cash the forged cheque. After some hesitation he consented to do so. He explained that under ordi- nary circumstances he would have declined to cash it, but that the young lady's air of respectability impressed him so greatly in her favour that he thought he was running no risk in" obliging " her. Those of his friends who were in court were astonished at his calm demeanour in the witness- box, but their astonishment reached its zenith when he proceeded to infer that he was a man of methodical habits. In the course of cross-examina- tion he stated that it was his custom occasionally to write down in a note-book, especially kept for that purpose, the dates on which he cashed cheques for customers, also the number of the cheque, the bank on which it was drawn, and other details connected with the matter. Sir Edward Masters asked that this "interesting book," as he sarcastically described it, should be produced in court. The prosecuting counsel at once agreed that it should be forthcoming at the trial. Gwendoline heard the word trial with a sinking heart. A dreamy feeling of despair stole over her. Not even in her most desponding moments had she imagined that the prosecution possessed evidence of such weight as was now being brought forward. With shrinking terror she realized to what end this condemnatory evidence must point. Little by little the fact that she was in the dock, the cynosure of hundreds of eyes,. faded from her mind. Her whole attention became riveted on the witness and his evidence. As the hearing proceeded it became evident, even to her legally ignorant mind, that the' witnesses for the prosecution were weaving a strong case against her. Anxiously; and with an aching heart, Mr. Treherne watched her growing pallor and the mental suffering' depicted 'on her face. Greater torture could not have been,infticted on hirn than being 'forced to remain an inactive spectator of her

misery. 'With tierce resentment Jae realized tnat tirace was out or danger and re,raming tier strength the strong arm of the law had interposed between satisfactorily, he began to consider matters from a him' and his much-beloved child. The fact,of different point of view. fatherhood availed mithim-, .now that she ,Vvt, As he stood in the hall brushing his hat in an accused of breaking the laws .of her country." ^ absent-minded manner, preparatory to leaving home, strove to keep his attention riveted on the evidenb„ his thoughts were such as he did not care to but whenever his eyeS wandered in the direction of, analyse. othing could have been more inoppor- the dock the sad, unhappy face of his beautiful-,- tune than his aunt's persistent manner of remind- daughter seemed to paralyze his powers of compre? ing'him that his wife was, comparatively speaking, hension. perfect. How deeply rooted in the human mind is Wearily the case dragged on. Five o'clock the spirit of contradiction. In his present mood struck, then six. At last there came a hush, he keenly resented having advice thrust upon him Tao magistrate was carefully scanning his notes. wholesale; but his affection for his aunt induced He glanced at Gviundoline regretfully. The counsel him to receive it with moderate patience. Had she for the prosecution rose and made some remark, adopted the opposite line of argument and spoken which caused Sir Edward Masters to rise and make scornfully of his wife, the latter's hold of his a terse reply. Gwendoline heard neither; she wa affections might have remained as strong—or, wondering, in a vague manner, what would happet speaking more correctly, as weak—as hitherto. next. Then the words "Committed for trial - Unhappily, he now regarded her from a very reached her ears, different point of view to what he had done on The hearing was over, and had ended as she their wedding day. Then he had entertained for feared, her that chivalrous feeling which a good, pure, and beautiful woman never fails to, call forth in the _ _

breast of a young and impressionable man. Not for a moment had he believed that she was aware of her father's shady transactions ; still less that she was implicated therein. Now, however, small doubt remained in his mind that she was aware not only who had forged the cheque, but who had uttered it; and, worse than that, his suspicions that she was implicated in the crime were growinp daily darker, for he recollected having beetle Captain Tewser refer to Richard Musgrove. The more he had thought over the matter—a,s_ there were few hours in which it was wholly absent from his mind—the more complicated appeared his connection with the case. To a man who prided himself upon his scrupulously honour- able career, the idea was very galling of his wife shielding from arrest those who had broken the laws of their country, and allowing an innocent person to be convicted. He recalled with shrink- ing horror Grace's strong affection far him and her slavish desire to please him and do his bidding. At that moment he would have preferred that she had been blessed—at least, cursed—with a fierce temper and an uncontrollable will. Then he would not have been haunted by fears of behaving in an unmanly manner to a sensitive and devoted wife, whose gentleness appealed for protection to his chivalrous instincts. One moment he felt that he could not face her pathetic fear of giving him offence, with that decisiveness which alone could force her to admit what part she had played in the forging and utter- ing of the cheque. The next moment his pride caused him to indignantly resent the idea that he, Dennis Vane, could fail to do his duty by not insisting on his wife confessing all she knew of the crime. As to the consequences— "Only cowards shirk doing what has to be done for fear of the consequences," he said to himself as he walked towards his chambers. Then 14 thought of his child, and his brows contracts... "Poor little thing! She will inherit a load 0. discreditable connections," he added. It was growing hourly clearer to him that he was called upon to act without prejudice in the matter of his wife's complicity. As if, in fact, Grace were not his wife and Gwendoline not the woman he had once dearly loved.
CHAPTER XXVIII. Consternation and dismay reigned in the Tre- herne's home. Until the conclusion of the hear-

ing before the magistrates, one and all the family had entertained the hope that, by some miraculous intervention, the prosecution would be crushed and Gwendoline acquitted. The moment Mr. Treherne re-entered the house, on that sadly-eventful day he explained to Mrs. Treherne and Constance exactly how matters stood, and his sorrow-stricken face had revealed but too clearly fears that his daughter—now a prisoner "out on bail "—was destined to enjoy only a few more weeks of liberty. Then had followed a wild scene of grief, in which Mrs. Treherne had played the principal part. With habitual inconsistency she had blamed the whole family individually and collectively for having, in some inexplicable manner, assisted in bringing the prosecution to a head. Time after time she stated, in a wailing voice, that the real forger and utterer would have been discovereA had her advice been acted upon from the beginnini_ "The whole world is up in arms against darling girl—l know it ' With this illoricai remark she had withdrawn to her room and had

not quitted it for a week. Meanwhile a deplorable change was stealing over Gwendoline. The delightful vivacity of manner had given way before the great weight of her trouble, and her expressive brown eyes now possessed a look of sadness, which infected all those on whom they rested with deep pity for one so sorely tried. The habit of slightly gesticulating with her small, shapely hands, and emphasizing amusing remarks had deserted her. Those clever hands that had done such good work in the past, and had been destined by their owner to do still better work in the future, lay limp and idle hour after hour on her lap, as the days passed wearily— yet only too fast. She knew that there was nothing she, person- ally, could do to avert her doom. The defence lay in the hands of shrewd lawyers, men skilled in the forms and technicalities of legal procedure. Nothing came within her province but inactivity and patient waiting. The pleasant sense of useful- ness which comes to those who are "up and doing," striving to right the wrong by manual or mental work, was denied her. In comparative solitude and ever-increasing hopelessness she was destined to pass the intervening days of her liberty. Armed with apparently circumstantial evidence as the prosecution was, she did not for an instant belieu it could fall through. The power to laugh seemi. to have gone from her; only when her father oi mother was present did she succeed in conjuring up a smile. With the quenching of her long- cherished hopes she had lost the power to do more than suffer in a passive, heart-broken manner. She was no coward, yet her spirit quailed at the idea of imprisonment. The thought of spending the precious moments of her youth, which should have been bright, happy and free, surrounded by the degrading circumstances of prison life, haunted her night and day. Earnestly she hoped that she would not survive her term of imprisonment. To expect her to re-enter the world and take up the broken threads of a life that had once promised to be brilliantly successful, and attempt good work labouring under the shadow of criminal antecedents, was asking her to exercise too great an effort of will. No if she were convicted—and she did not doubt that she would be—she earnestly hoped that God in His mercy would let her pass away, unnoticed by her friends, within the gloomy prison walls. Thus the time sped by. Only a week remained before the trial, and, as usually was the case now, Mr. Treherne had returned early from his office in order to have a quiet time before dinner with Gwendoline. They were not talking of the forthcoming trial— a tacit understanding existed that the subject was only to be referred to when there was some speck, reason for mentioning it. "There is one thing I should like to do this week, father," Gwendoline began with hesitation. "Yes," he answered kindly; 'what is it? " "It is this. I should like to go to the Academy and take a last peep at my picture." Her voice quivered as she uttered the concluding words. "I will take you there to-morrow, dear," was the reply. "We will not stay long. I should like to walk there and back, and to go quite early so that we may escape seeing anyone we know." You shall have your way, my child." Mr. Treherne spoke as if he were glad that it still lay in his power to gratify her wishes. Then the conversation drifted to other subjects. Although it was only half-past nine, when the Trehernes arrived at the Academy on the follow- ing morning, the galleries were by no means empty. Clusters of genuine sight-seers were stand- ing round the favourite works of the year, and everyone present had an air of having come "to do ' the Academy with businesslike precision—not to study the attires of the other visitors. The Trehernes walked quickly through the galleries, only casting cursory glances at the pictures until they approached Gwendoline's, around which about two dozen people were crowded. A bright look of gratification instantly stole over her face, for she noticed that many regarded it with evident approval. "We will wait until some of those people thy away," she whispered to her father as she sat dowel by the side of a good-natured looking person, whose st 3, is of dress announced that she was from the country. A moment later two girls detached themselves from the group round the picture and joined her. "Oh! mother, you ought to look at Hope's Achievement 'I" said one of them. "The girl's face is lovely—so full of tenderness." "I -am tired to death of looking at pictures," was the uninterested reply. "But when yon get, home everybody will ask you if you saw Miss Treherne's picture. Her trial ta.kes place next week."

"CM 1,1 didn't understand that you wanted me to look at the picture which the young person who forged that cheque painted," she answered, rising with alacrity and walking passed her daughters. Then, with amusing sangfroid she edged her way' through the crowd and planted herself in front of the picture. "Very sad case," Gwendoline's sharp ears just - then detected a gentleman near saying to a friend. "Her people are in an excellent position, and, as you say, she is a very talented artist." "Yes," agreed the other, "and would probably have risen to eminence had it not been for this prosecution. Of course, she may be acquitted." His manner inferred much doubt on the subject. "She may be, of course; but the general idea is that she is guilty. I don't see how a doubt can be entertained on the subject." By this time the old lady had finished scruti- nizing the picture and rejoined her dal, ghters. "A girl who could paint a picture like that one," she observed as they moved away, "ought to have been above going about trying to get a forged cheque cashed. But some girls are born wicked, and it's of no use trying to teach them to do what's right. I have heard that that dreadful man Peace, who murdered one or two policemen, was very good at musi , and a domestic character at heart. The world is a terribly bad place, and I don't doubt but that this young lady artist allowed herself to be made a tool of by some designing man, who has left her to face the trial alone. "I hope it will be proved that she is innocent," said the elder girl. "Oh, well, it's a disgraceful affair, and she won't ever be able to hold her head up very high after the trial, whichever way it goes," replied her mother.

--Crwen-doline had remained in her seat, listening, fascinated by the novelty of hearing herself dis- cussed by total strangers. "How cruel How unjust the world is I" she mentally exclaimed, in bitterness of spirit. At that moment the people clustered round her picture separated. She rose quickly and took one long, loving look at the work on which she had lavished so many earnest, pleasurable hours; then turned away with a deep-drawn sigh. • "We will go home now, father," she said in a low voice.
Pathetically sad was her expression as they retraced their steps through the galleries.
(To be cmtinued.)

div.head: CHAPTER XXVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVII.

The matter -of - fact manner in which Mrs. Hughes discussed the hearing of Gwendoline Treherne's case before the magistrates annoyed Dennis beyond measure. Finding it impossible to elicit from him any information respecting it, she procured and read the account in the Moe fling Post during breakfast. This was unprecedented conduct on her part, for she even rigorously sup- pressed the opening of letters until this meal was nearly over. However, her curiosity in this case would brook no delay, and she read sometimes to herself and sometimes out loud, in that aggravat- ing manner with which many people transmit news. "Dear me! What dreadful disclosures!" she exclaimed, putting the newspaper down for a moment as she poured herself out a cup of coffee. "To think that this dishonourable person was left in your uncle's charge! Happily, I studiously avoided mentioning the matter to anyone in our own neighbourhood. What an opportune circum- stance was the arrival of that telegram summoning you home. I was very distressed about it at the time, but I feel grateful now for anything whicti served to distract your attention from a certalr quarter. How shocked your uncle will be! I hope he will not talk to the parishioners about our having met these Trehernes abroad. I must send him a copy of to-day's newspaper and tell him to be discreet. But he never reads the police news. Just remind me, Dennis, to put a cross against the column, otherwise he will only read the crick—l mean, at least, the ecclesiastical intelligence." "Why does he not run up to London for a few days? " said Dennis, hoping to turn the current of his aunt's thoughts. "All men who live in the country, especially clergymen, should make a point of spending a week in London during the season. It keeps them au courant with new phases of thought and— "Positively the same dress she wore sometimes at Les Avants," interrupted Mrs. Hughes, who had not heard a word her nephew was saying. "Guilty —she must be guilty! " With these words she put down the newspaper and looked interrogatively at him. "I could stake my life that she is not," he answered solemnly. "Happily she is not a mother. Young men can- not be too careful whom they marry in these degenerate days. Imagine the harassing position of a man whose wife was in the habit of forging! ' She could sign deeds of settlement on herself, and ho would soon find his affairs in a most oomph cited state. As to this unfortunate girl, that really seems to be no excuse for her conduct. But I must say that she ought to have chosen a married man's name to forge. I suppose she imagined that you would take no steps in the matter, as of course—" She stopped abruptly and coughed. "Neither have I." "I observe with astonishment that you are bail for her in a thousand pounds. I must say Ido not approve of your acting so indiscreetly. People will talk, Dennis--they will talk." "Let them ! " he replied, curtly and angrily. It was mental agony to listen to his aunt rambling on in this condemnatory vein. "I am genuinely sorry for Miss Treherne," he continued. "I only wish it were in my power to put an end to her prosecution If she is condemned it will be a scandalous miscarriage of justice! " Mrs. Hughes pressed her lips together in an ominous manner, then observed in a very decided tone, "I am quite shocked to hear you talk like that. In my opinion it nearly borders on immor- ality. Indeed, it does, Dennis. You ought to uphold the punishment of evil doers, instead of which you are positively siding with one who ought to have known better than to be a patty to uttering

a forged cheque." Mrs. Hughes was silent for a few minutes, as if gathering up her thoughts for further reflections on the subject. Then she placed her hand on Dennis's arm. "My boy," she began persuasively, and summoning all her latent powers of eloquence "I wish you would withdraw yourself entirely from the society of the Trehernes. Think of your dear wife and sweet little child. Do not forget the solemnity of such responsibilities. It is pot correct of you to allow your thoughts to centre round Miss Treherne. I quite hoped you had got over your foolish weakness in that direction, hut I fear you have not. lam sure your uncle will be very shocked at your present conduct. He never thinks of anyone else but me—at least, of course, in that kind of way, though I am sure the manner in which Miss Drew lays herself out to attract his attention in church is most unseemly. What a much purer, holier place the world would be if all women were born ugly!" "Heaven forbid! emphatically exclaimed Dennis. "You should see Miss Drew's bonnets!" con- tinued his aunt. . . . •

"I have, and thought them curious; but they certainly suit her. She is rather prPtty, you know, aunt." Ile made this last remark in a manner which announced he wished to open out a new topic of conversation. "Curious! That does not half describe their outrageous vulgarity. But, dear me! I was tall;ing about Miss Treherne's prosecution. I wish, Dennis, you would not distract my attention. I want you to be sensible over the matter, and not to try and stand between her and justice." "But I know Miss Treherne did not forp

name, and--" "My dear Dennis, you know nothing of the kind. You are merely arguing yourself into believing you do; which, of course, is just nonsense! A girl with a pretty face can make a man believe any- thing. I don't doubt that she has thrown lie•self upon your mercy and declared she never uttered that cheque—but she did! Mark my words. What sensible person could doubt it? Now that she has been recognised by two respectable people who are willing to swear that she is the forger--," "No; the person who uttered the cheque—excuse -my contradicting you, aunt," interrupted Dennis. "Which requires a person to be quite as wicked and unscrupulous as forging it. Imagine what a barefaced person she must be to go from shop to shop asking people to cash it I A quiet, retiring, sweet-minded woman—like your wife for instance" —Dennis shuddered and looked away—"would rather die than do such things. But, honestly speaking, I am not the least surprised to hear that Miss Treherne has behaved so badly. What else could be expected of a young person of her worldly stamp ?" "She is the victim of a conspiracy—a deeply- laid, disgraceful conspiracy I " said Dennis, indig- nantly; "and it would take a great load off my mind•if I could discover the conspirators." "In my opinion the interest you show in wishing to prove Miss Treherne innocent is greatly to your discredit. With an angelic wife—for Grace is most affectionate, clinging woman I know, • she adores you and the baby—with an angelic wife. I repeat, you ought never to let your thoughts wander from your home." "My interest ;n Miss Treherne's trial is such as no honourable man need be ashamed of," answered Dennis, colouring. Then, with a view to cutting 'short this distasteful conversation, he hastily con- cluded his breakfast, rose from the table, and left , the room. . .

Grace was better. "Rapidly regaining her strength," so the nurse, who was waiting in the hall to give him the latest news, informed him with a glow of satisfaction, adding that "in another week Mrs. Vane ought to be downstairs, and a.t week later going about as usual." "A week later "—three weeks from the present moment. As Dennis heard this remark he realised that perhaps he would be able to reopen the subject of the forged cheque with his wife, and make one final attempt to gain information from her before .the trial of Gwendoline Treherne took place. His wife's rapid recovery, had removed from his mind the harassing fear that the exciting conver- sation, of the night when she was taken ill, might lead to fatal results. Ho had thought with con- siderable contrition over that conversation, and had constantly blamed himself for speaking with thoughtless severity on the occasion. But now that

div.head: LEGEND OF THE EAST.

It was not Cor- 02:treat Sewers poration property, and they would make themselves 2,651 10 1 2,237 06 2,267 18 1 liable to a civil action for trespass by the Manchester Ship Canal Company if they were to enter it.lt was not the site of the intended cloaks at all. From a health point of view the best course to take would be to fill it up. Solid matter held in suspension was carried to this , portion 01 the river, and as there was no through pas- sage it became gradually deposited in the bed, and would continue to be deposited there as long as it was kept open. If they took out the present sludge by dredging they would have to continue dredging, and the condi- tion of the river would be no better. He thought the best plan would be to fill up as far as Wilderspool in the best'manner that engineers could devise. He hadn't t e slightest sympathy with the suggestion of doing what Councillor Bennett had proposed, because the Corpora- tion had no power in the matter. (Hear, hear.) (jonncidor Suess. GREEN said:—The Council will be glad to know that eee are approaching the time when all our public OffleeS will be close togyher. We have now got the order permitting the overseers to lent a p)rtion of the premises known as Bank House, and both the poor and improvement rate will be payable at one place in the future. • It has been deemed advisable to sotn-what vary ' the old method of presenting the estimates. Hitherto each chairman has presented and given the details of his own special committee, and explained the cause of any serious differences in comparison with that of previous years. The estimates are now to be put ' before us as a whole in one formal resolution, and per- haps the advantage of the change may be that it will give the opportunity of taking a more comprehensive view of our local expenditure. and probably saiAa much time. As seen to-day, the" Budget," to call it by its new, name, does seem a seething Man of figures, but the method of their presentation will, I think, commend it- self. Lest some of our number who may fairly be called our outspoken members shiouid imagine this is 'another "device" of the Chairman of the Finance Committee, let me say at once, the change is frit mine, hut has been put into this form by our responsible advisers as more in accordance with modern usage and simplicity of ar- raneement. Figures and fluance are not at any time an attractive subject, but certainly there is no subject of more importance to us at the present. Before proceed. Ins, with the estimates let UP spend a moment or two in considering the transactions of, the past year. Generally the committees have kept fairly within their 'estimates, but it is impossible not b note one or two. The Wateh Committee, the first on our list, is conspicu- ous for having again "overrun the constable." The Town Hall, Park, and Baths has overspent upon every head of its estimate where it could. The Hospital De- partment, from which owing to the fortunate absence of epidemic we expected a considerable saving, has spent almost £lOO over, its estimates. The other and last committee to be enumerated is the Fire Engine Coin- mitten. This appears to be in need of some supervision, for out of 11 heads of expenditure it has over spent upon seven. Notwithstanding savings in some committees we have in the aggregate overspent ourselves, and had .it not been for two or three fortunate circumstances wihich I propose to detail shortly we Should have had a different store to tell. These circumstances are the et- ceptional rehires from the sale of manure at Longford. a sustained increase in the market toil e, and an increase In the revenue fr ern the baths and weights and measures. 'But the most important is the steady and sustained e improvement rate. This has brought .ignronwoth of h than £603 over the amount put down. The only &pertinent that on paper has not shown the same elasticity nee yet chme up to its expected amount is the Cenaltery,from which we anticip tted £1,120 It has realised £1,119 181.71., but lam informed this may, be accounted for in par' by a reduoed death rate, and to the fact that the extension of the borough has reduced the burial fees to a large number of the inhahitents. Corning now to the estimates for the ensuing year. These occupying the first 14 pages of the Budget may appear difficult to grasp in all their detail, but they will be found focuseed on page 15 Taking them as they appear the Borough Rate section claims attention first. This estimate in the aggregate is £2,618 less than last year, but it does not arise so much from a reduced exp-endi- bre as from the fact that the tares debit balance his been broueht from £2,420 to £260. Ido not want to weary the Councieand therefore it is not my purpose to deal with each. I shall refer only to those which from any special cause demand attention. The Watch CJM- mitten asks for an extra £289, but of this the men's nay absorbs the major part. The General Purposes Committee asks for £5O less. I ex- pected better things from this committee, but the Council has already senctioned theln, zcluins. nianitsi esti- mate of two unexpected items, viz Instal- ment of the cost of the wood pavement in front ef the Parr Hall, and £250 as a guarantee fund for an Art Exhibition. The Cemetery Committee asks for an extra £265. They tell us they must have a new greenhouse. Well, the cemetery, though the subject of many painful memories, is yet a place greatly frequentel,and we can- net avoid the appeal to make it as attractive as possible. Most ef us will be glad to see that the Town Hall Corn- Committee has finished its expensive furnishing and al- terations, and that we have a call for £5BO less. The School Attendance Committee wants £lOO extra, but as this is entirely for the maintenance and training of blind and dumb children, none will complain who realise the great benefit to the community as well se to the children this special training gives. It was antici- pated that with the absence from the present estimates of the £5OO voted to the Mayor last year, the Finance Committee might have come with a substantial reduc- tion, but extra printing— which item, by the way, is in- creasing at a rapid rate—lefisieney of the rate in the newly added area, and salaries chargeable to this depart- ment have brought the reduction down to £220 only The total estimate, as I hive already said, is a reduction In the aggregate of £2,818, and therefore we have to ask the Overseers for a sum which should allow of a re- duced peer rate by 41. in the £. Having dealt with the Borough Rate, we now come to the Improvement Rate. This unfortunately is the opposite of the Borough Rate, for the amount required for the purposes of this account is £21,246, or £621, more than last year. The increase Is spread over the entire list of the committees with the exception of the Health Committee, It is almost im- possible to particularize, but the item of wages may be credited with a good deal of the increase. Our extended area has naturally entailed increased work in the various sanitary departments,and more men have been pet on to meet the extra demand, We also feel now in practical form the extra cost of our street improvement acriount, this item alone requiring nearly £5OO extra. The Long- ford Depot Department claims special notice for its last three items. The first of the three being interest on its extension—the way of dealing with this capital expendi- ture has yet to be settled—and the other two being £lOO for a shaping machine and £5OO for a new dryer. Ido net know what a shaping machine is but perhape the Chairman of the Sanitary Works Committee will surplaies The Highway Department wants £859 more, the &lint items being permanent paving and material, and a sum of £2OO on account of a crane. Then lastly we have the Markets Committee asking for an additional £lOO to help to make up the charge for painting the ball and shed. The receipts coming to the credit of this expendi- ture show little advance upon last year,so that if it had not been for the special relief 1 shall mention shortly this rate must have gone tip considerably. The only other estimate which is submitted separately, is the Sewers Rate. Last year we were compelled to ask for £2,237, We were in debt to the bank, and had to levy a rate at 41. in the 2. It has been our custom to levy this rate alternately of 41. and 21., but I am afraid the day for this is past, and in the future we may only occasionally get a rate at 21. The sewerine of the ex- tension of our bouneary will for a long period cost us a considerable Inns, and though this year we have caved something and have a balance in the bank of £209, our estimate is £2,287, and we shall therefore have to ask you again for a 4d. rate. In the Borough Rate we only have the power to make a can upon the Overseers, and with that our business ends, but with respect to the Improvement Rate whatever increase there is we get the benefit of it. The elaeticity of our revenue bas been explained,hut the thing that has halF,ss us is a premiss from the Gas De- partment. It will be in the recellectien of the Council that ire a recent memorable debate I stated the Finance Commit tee had requested the Gee Department to give them as a first charge upon the profits £1,500 in aid of the Improvement Rate. To enable us to feel the pulse of nut expenditure we have a tabulated monthly return, and the request for the £1,500 was based on an estimate of oar deficieney and anticipated needs. lam sorry te say that at the close the result was not so "rosy" as we had reason to hops. The Gas Department, by the minutes passed to-night, has shown a readiness to accede to our request,and it is my pleasure to be able to say,with this help we can face the extra expenditureoind levy a rate at the same am•unt FtS last year. In doing this,we sincerely trust each member of the Council will consider himself boisnd by every hon- ourable tie to sustain the estimates and avoid any over- running of the expenditure. We have great schemes be- fore es, and some people ask if our financial position justifies the attempt to carry them all out. Well, I think so. We have a growing rateable value,three exception- ally good sources of revenue,and, rightly used, we have no need to be apprehensive as to the future. We have, to all appearances, also a friendly feeling on the official pile tl-tP L Government Board. Let u, do nothing to lose that, for they have it in their power

At a meeting of this committee a letter was read from the Science and Art Department, saying that the In- spector who recently visited the School of Art had " re- ported favourably upvn the conduct, discipline, and work of the School." It was reported that arrangements bad been made to provide a cookery centre at which classes from the Day schools would attend, and it was resolved that the room over the Plumbing Room at the School ef Science be appropriated for this purpose, and that a sum not exceeding £4O be spent in cleaning, re- pairs, and apparatus; and that the thanks of the Corn. mittee be given to Nies ors. --- Apropos of meteorites the following amusing story is told by Sir Robert Ball respecting one of these celestial visitors. A meteorite which fell on a farm in America was claimed by the ground landlord,as his lease reserved all minerals and metals. The tenant objected on the score that the article was not on the property when the lease was executed. The landlord then claimed it as flying game, but the lessee pleaded that the thing had neither feathers nor wings and claimed it as ground gams. But while the dispute was going on, the customs officers seized the meteorite on the ground that the revenue had been defrauded by its introduction into the country without payment of duty.

Canada apparently still frets under the title of " Our Lady of the Snows," bestowed upon her by Mr. Boat- yard Kipling. Accordingly, under the title of " Our Lady of the Sunshine " we. are to have a Canadian mid- summer annual this year, in which the bright and sunny aspects of the Dominion are to be emphasised by local poets, novelists, essayists, and artists. No doubt, the one title is as correct as tbe other. A trip across the continent from Quebec to Vancouver between June and September shows the country in almost topical radi- ance, but the same journey between November and April SillOW/1 a dreary and depressing expanse of univer- sal snow. Mr. Kipling is right in winter, and the forth- coming annual will be perfectly correct in summer.

The latest development of militant patriotism in the United States is one which the children of that great country may possibly view with less fervor than its promoters. It is that a battleship to replace the Maine at a cost of a million sterling, shall be raised by sub- scriptions of one cent a week from the children in the various public schools throughout the country. As there are probably about 10,000,000 children attending theee schools, it would require nearly a year to raise the sum.

"Lele-majestiS "in China Seems to be an even more fearsome •ffence than it is in German!. The " Peking Gazette" announces the condemnation for this criml of one None.tzi, a reckless journalist, who, in referring to the careers of certain historical Emperors, omitted to add to their names the full titles to which they are en- titled according to Celestial etiquette. The offender was speedily reminded of his forgetfulness, and was sent- enced to undergo the penalty of high treason, involving something exceedingly unpleasant in the way of punish- ment, in which all his children were to share. With unusual clemency, however, the Son of Heaven com- muted this punishment to simple decapitation; and the Chinese Conservatives are Said to be even more distressed by the weakness of their Imperial Master than by any recent concessions to "foreign devils." German offenders must be trembling lest the Kaiser's sudden enthusiasm for China should tempt him to graft the Celestial cus- tom on to German jurisprudence.

"AN UrTER FRAUD."

Betore Messrs. R. Garnett, and T. Birchall at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, John Morley, of Weston, appeared on remand charged with beg- ging by means of a letter purporting to be written by George Sedgwick,Rose Cottage, Weston Point.—The Chiet Constable said that he had made snquiries and found that no such person as George Sedgwick was known at Weston Point, though there was a Rose Cottage. He found that prisoner had alto- gether been convicted for vazrancy, drunkenness, 'etc., 41 times. He had beer cmvic;ed 11 times for begging, twice for obtaining money by false pre- tences, five times for begging by fraud as on this occasion, end 26 times for drunkenness and sleep- ing out. The police everywhere seemed to know him. He was an utter fraud. Prisoner: If you please. your Worships, I should like to say I have been remanded for a week. I went to the grocer's shop with the paper but made no use of it. My character has been a bad one, but lam an old man. I have done no harm either in the sight of God or the laws of my country. I will leave Warrington and never come into the town again.: _ . .
The manager of the shop where prisoner pre- sented his paper wes called to prove that he did make use of it. Witness gave him 6cl.

Prisoner:lf you Will kindly be lenient with me, I will promise in the sight of God that I will never write anything like that again. I at 62 years of age. The Chief Constable added that prisoner bad alto- gether spelot about three years in prison. Just lately they ;lad had several complaints of begging- letter imp,stors. One man had thv audacity to present a letter purporting to come from an emin- ent clergymen in this district.
, The bench sent prisoner to gaol for a month with hard labour.

div.head: EXAM IN Ell ,
div.p: THE EXAM IN Ell ,
APRIL 7th, 1898.

The great gathering in the House Poreign AC:airs. of Commons on Tuesday after- noon to hear a statement of Mr. tailor:Jß upon the political complications of the I°ar East was a fairly accurate indication of the anxiety that is widely felt at the present time With reference to foreign affairs. Alike in the East and the West te prospects are far from being as pacific as could be wished. At the time of writing an armed conflict between the United States and Spain over the Cuban question appears to be inevitable, and this in itself is enough to disturb the Political outlook. When there is, as some writers put it, so much combus- tible material lying about, it does not require a large spark to raise a gencral conflagration. On the whole, however, the chances are in favour of the localisation, so to speak, of a war between the States and Spain. If it does come to fighting in the end, the best thing that could happen Would be the w.nning of a decisive naval victory by the Americans. Once the American people ,fairlY enter upon the work of liberat- ing Cuba it may be taken for granted that they will persist in it till they have completed their whole programme. If, therefore, a few early successes were to be scored bY the Spaniards they would only have the effect of prolonging a contest the issue of which is prac- tically a foregone conclusion. On the other hand, if the American navy is able to assert its supre- taaey from the very commencement, even the Proud Spaniard must realise that the game is .up ee far as Cuba is concerned. The large attendance at the House of Commons on Tuesday was, how-

ever, not drawn together by the doings of either the Americans or Spaniards or Cuban insurgents ' hUt by the latest developments in China. Mr. liALrouit as the leader of the House, and as Lord 4Lissuny's locum tenens, had promised to give a tilllch-needed explanation of the situation before the House adjourned for the Easter holidays. It Cannot be said that the explanation has added ranch to the puulic knowledge of the events of the last few months, nor will it tend to allay the anxiety which is felt as to the preservation of British commercial interests in the Far East. In one sense Mr. BALFoun's statement is dis- tinctly disquieting, as it helps to confirm the suspicion that our Government has not even ya fixed upon a settled policy with re- gard to the Chinese question, There is,as several Speakers pointed out, a good deal of danger to be apprehended from this condition of uncertainty. Other countries—Russia and Germany for instance —know what they want to be at and aim straight at their mark. The British Government alone appears to be hesitating and waiting for some- thing to turn up. The result is a loss of prestige, and there are few who will not agree with Sir EDWARD birV.F.,Y when he said that a loss of prestige in the East a serious matter for a world-wide erepire, oven from a commercial point of view alone. Our Government, through not having a Clearly defined policy of its own, is having its hands forced by other Powers some of which are none too friendly. The Russians having obtained Port Arthur, the British Minister at Pekin has ob- tained from the Chinese authorities a concession 14 another port, Wei-Hai-Wei, when that port is evacuated by the Japanese who are at present in Doasession. Yet nobody seems to know what Ilse. can be made of this latest acquisition. t not likely that it will be of much commercial tane hi time of peace, and in case of a war with "-Inasia, for instance, or indeed with any power ,that could attack it, the place will either have to ce abandoned or defended by a force which will be llkrently needed elsewhere. While talking about t transaction in the House of Comm.ms, Mr. :11rtne.y recalled the case of Cyprus. The acquire- of that island was defended by a former ery government on the ground that it would be atiCther bulwark of the empire.lt was to be made a rat place of arms, and to thoroughly establish ritish supremacy in the Mediterranean. Yet Cyprus is now so meanly thought of by military entherities that it is, we bel;eve, garrisoned by a ai4gle company of British troops. Even in a cmumercial sense it cannot be regarded as a very brilliant jewel in the imperial crown, for the inhabitants protest that they are now more heavily taxed than they were when under the rule of the Sulaax. On the whole there is good reason for thinking that Wei-Hai-Wei is simply another acquisition of the Cyprus type. The Government tirtt is now in power in this country have suffered so many diplomatic defeats that they have been 'driven into doing something, wisely or unwisely, by the dissatisfied clamours of their own followers. In this case they have probably acted U.nwisely and they have added one more complies- -Imm to a very complication position of affairs.

Tux dispute in the Welsh Another 4-dionur Dispute. coal trade bids fair to lead to another extensive labour c on- '• In this instance even more workmen will be anoctea than by the engineers lock-out, but the *4llggle will be more localised. The Welsh miners 4Pear to have been driven into something like a 41,11ontaneou5 revolt by the hardships of their lot. eir wages have been regulated by a sliding scale Oh the result that in many cases they have :111 earned a living wage. They now demand 1,11 increase in their pay of about twenty per cent. e demand has been refused by nearly all the LkploYers and as things now stand there does not 'nok to be any room for conciliation. Their organisation is evi- tlY of a very slender description and, unlike the :f iill,l°Yors, they have no accumulated funds to Cask upon. The unanimity of the miners in 51fa'etion they have now taken is evidence in A- ID' ttiat the grievances they complain of have itle3l widely felt ;at the same time it is clear that, pi:Pita of the enthusiasm and solidarity now dis- -Yedi there is a hard time in front of the wives ter° families of these Welsh collliers. The mas- „tors' °o the other hand, are well prepared for the ~,,,nflict• They have anticipated the crisis and pro- for it.
