THE FORTHCOMING nix OF WORE. In *connection with the Mersey Mission to Seamen Runcorn Branch,a two days sale of work is to be opened in the mission room on Wednesday and Thursday, April 20th and 21st. Particulars are advertised,

ST. EDWARD'S RUNCORN. At this church on Sunday, EDWARD'S, Rev. Father Ryan of St. Mary's, Middlewich, took the place of the pastor, the Rev. Father Gore. Father Ryan, who has been the insane of starting funds in Birkenhead, Wallasey, and Liverpool, in aid of the distress in Ireland, spoke on the famine at the services at St. Edward's.—On Monday a dance will be held in the Public Hall, Runcorn. Tickets are being sold at Is. 61. single, and 2s. 61. dowels, and may be had where the small handbills are exhibited. SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE, RUNCORN. At the ram:ably meeting of the "Open Sunday school," held at the Institute on Sunday afterneen,the choir sang " Along the river " and " The Golden Gate." Mr. Tom Wood gave "Only to know," and Mr. F. Mack was heard to distinct advantage in" The Lost Chord" and "Nazareth." Mr. G. Forster accompanied the various items. During the afternoon two bibles were presented for regular attendance and good conduct.

BETHESDA P.S.A., RuNconw. Mr. F. Beck presided over the weekly meeting of the above society on Sunday afternoon. The speaker for the day was the Rev. Samuel Wright. Mr. Bro leek of Widnes rendered with fine feeling and expression the respective solcn of " Nazareth " and "Calvary." Miss Phcehe Humphries sang "The Better Land" with superb affect. A selection of music on the organ,the "Elallelujah Chorus " (given by special desire) by Mr. Calvert organ- ist of the Congregational Church,Southampton, received the warm plaudits of the large audience.

BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. On Sunday afternoon the usual interim Foreign Mis- sionary meeting was held. Mr. N. Dodd was in the chair and very efficiently presided over what became a very interesting meeting. The report for the past five moathe was read by Mr. John Bireett and showed the antount subscribed in the classes and collected with books by some of the scholars amounted to £32 185.4 d., being an increase of 7s. 11d, ever the corresponding period of last year. Mr.Hogg who has spent some years in Egypt and other Eastern lands gave a very able addreselon Foreigh Missionary work, which was listened to throughout with marked attention. Tue R •v. R. J. Clifton also spoke for a few minutes after which a col- lection was made which realised £2 7s. 61., making a total of £35 55. 10d. BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCIOOL. The annual meeting of the trrichers of this, the eldest school in the town, was held on Monday night. The Rev. E. W. L. Christian in the chair. The General Secretary presented the statistical report showing that there were 66 officers and teachers and 460 scholars on the books with an average afternoon attendance of 39 and 334 respectively. The treasurer's report showed a balance in hand of £l7 10s. 6el: The following were the officers appointed for the ensuing year, superintendents, Messrs. T. Sitnister and E.Taylor ; secretary to the com- mittee Mr. F. J. Norman J.P. ; treasurer, Mr. A. R. Nor- man J.P. ; school secretaries, Messrs. J. Unsworth, J. Birkett and J. Povah ; absentee visitors. Messrs. G. H. Kirkham, U.D.C, J. Jones, Nancollis and Pickthall. RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD MONTHLY MEETINE. The monthly meeting of the Runcorn Sohool Board was held on Tuesday evening in the Board-room at the Town Hall, Runcorn. Mr. J. Pritchard presided There were also present the Rev. Canon Wood, Messrs. F. J. Norman, JP., S. Taylor, J.P., E. Liaison, C.C., and Mr. Moss (acting clerk).—The School Attendance Committee reported that the number of parents summoned at the three meetings held, num- bered 67, and fifty-nine put in an appearance. The visitors reported that the number of scholars on the books was 3,345 as compared with 3,394 in March last year. a decrease of 49. The average attendance was 2,843 as against 2,749 in March last year an increase of 94. The percentage of attendance was 85 against 81 in the corresponding period of last year.—The report was considered very satisfactory.—The Chairman moved that notice be given to the Wesleyan Trustees that the Board would give up possession of the Brunswick school on the 31st July. He also moved that notice be given Co Messrs. J. R. and B. Leach terminating a tenancy of a class room at Granville-street school on 30th September. Mr. Norman seconded and they were carried.

THE HEALTH OF RUNCORN IN 1897. ANNUAL REPORT OF THE MEDICAL OFFICER. Dr. McDougall, medical officer of health, in his annual report for the year ended December 31st, 1897, which was submitted at the monthly meeting of the Urban Council this morning states that the number of deaths from all causes registered within the authority's sanitary district during the year 1897 amounted to 338 as compared with 268 for 1896, and 390 for 1895. The infant death roll of one year and under heads the list and amounts to 108. an increase of 28 on the pre- vious year,and a dezrease of 19 as compared with 1895. The death rate has unfortunately to be estimated again on a further reduction of population end I am credibly Informed that it would be a fair estimate to place the population as at Midsummer at 17,500. This abnormal state of things is entirely due to the scarcity of employ- ment, a number of families being compelled to leave the town to seek work elsewhere. Taking 17,500 as the basis of calculation, the death rate for the year would be 193 per thousand of the estimated population, and of the 15 deaths classified under the head of injuries be deducted the death rate would be 18.4 Five hundred and eighty- three births were registered during the year. Two hun- dred and forty-ive births in excess of deaths. Six hun- dred and twenty births were registered during 1896. The birth rate for 1897 would be 333, according to the estimated population. Referring to the outbreak of diphtheria,Dr. McDougall seem, it is difficult to account for the sudden onset of the outbreak at a time when most people were rejoicing and making merry over the Diamond Jubilee Day. Three or four dais prior to the Jubilee Day it rained very heavily and the subsoil became thoroughly soaked. Jubilee day was intensely hot, making pedestrianism for young children on that day very fatiguing, and mewing about on a soaked soil, they became peculiarly liable, in their exhausted physical condition, to attacks of this kind. Curiously enough, within a few days of the procession. several of the children that took nart in it sickened of this disease, and between the 21st and 30th of June seventeen notifications were received, and the rate of moratality for that and the two succeeding imonths was exceedingly high ; but it must not be as- sumed that the outbreak was wholly due to this cause, if at all due to it, although unfortunately the outbreak was concurrent with it. I fear, however, that we shall have to look to a cause of much longer standing to account chiely for the outbri ak and its continuance, viz.:—the sewage-soaked condition of the subsoil, and defective drains. These are legacies that have been handed down to the authority,and although every effort is being made to cope with this terrible evil, it will take some time yet before the one is eradicated and the other remedied • for scarcely a drain that is opened that does not reveal' the grossest carlessness and ignorance.which in some instances, amounts to criminal responsibility. Imperfect workmanship, in this respect, lass a great deal to answer for; and although the authority is doing good work in trying to overcome the errors of former years, there still remains much to be done. The substitution of water carriage is making slow progress; but it is the best and most natural method of disposing of human filth, and.! am assured by the present surveyor, that great care is being taken that when water-closets are connected with old drains, the latter undergoes rigorous and careful examination be- fore the connection is made. If this were not so, in all probability the end would be worse than the beginning. Syphoning of drains, and sewer and drain ventilation are also receiving attention. The infant rate of mortality is painfully high, but it is difficult to suggest a remedy Ahnut one-third of the entire death-roll for the twelve months are infants of one year or under. 108 deaths of infants of one year or under were registered during the year— That is about one infant to every five born succumbed within the year of its birth. The average infant death- rate for 1298 was much the same : but the birth-rate was -higher. and it will pork out to about one death to every seven births- The mortality of children of one year and under five years is also very high,and compares unfavourably with 1896. The increased death-rate ever 1896 is due to whooping cough, which was very preva- lent during the first seven months of the year, and to diptheria and measles, which were also prevalent about mid-summer, and to an increase of ten deaths from heart disease over the previous year, to an increase of twelve from diarrhoea and dysentery, and to an increase of six from bronchitis and its allied diseases over 1896. There is also a slight increase in the death rate from the un- classified diseases; but there is also a decrease in some of the classified, and some are unrepresented.

FARM FIRE AT MOORE. Information was' received at the Wilderspool Brewery at about 9.15 a.m. on Tuesday morning that a fire bad broken out on the farm premises of Mr. Percival, Moss Side Farm, Moore, and a steam engine and full complement of men were in a few minutes on their way to the spot. They found the , outbuildings in flames, and quickly got a good supply of water from the canal, a distance of about 470 yards. After pouring water on the flames for about three hours, they managed to subdue th.m, The damage is estimated at £4OO, and is covered by insurance. Fortunately thee were no cattle in the buildings at the time.

div.head: "IS RUNCORN A. PORT?"
div.p: "IS RUNCORN A. PORT?"

On Saturday, in the Queen's Bench Division, before Mr. Justice Day and Mr. Justice Bruce,the case in re an arbitration between Goodbody v. Balfour, Williamson and Co., came on for hearing. Mr. Bray, Q.C., and Mr. R. Bray were for Messrs. J. and L. Goodbody, co. Clare,corn merchants; and Mr. J. Walton, Q.C., end Mr. Danckwerte were for Messrs. Balfour, Williamson and Co., of Liverpool. The case raised a question as te the position of Runcorn as a commercial port, and Man- chester as a " safe port." Mr. Bray, Q.C., said this was an application by , Messrs. Goodbody to set aside an award on the ground of serious irregularities. The question arose out of a contract for the sale of a cargo of Walla Walla wheat, and the amount mentioned was from £3,000 to £4,000. On the 29th December, 1898, Messrs. Goodbody entered late a (thence party with Messrs. Balfour, Williamson and Co , for the purchase from them of 13,000 quarters of Walla Walla wheat, shipped on the Vanduava at £33 10s. for 61100 lbs, to any "safe port " in the U.K., or ' certain ports on the continent,as ordered by the buyers. ,On the 7th January the sellers rendered a provisional invoice of the cargo. On the Ist of that month the do- , cutnents representing the cargo were inspected byMessrs ' Goodbody to see if they were in order. By the charter party the port of Manchester was ex- eluded from the poris to which the ship could be sent. Messrs. Goodbody refused to take up the document, and subseq ently tile sellers, with- out consulting theta, induced the owners of the ship to agree to cancel the excluaion of the part of Manchester. On the 9th March the locuments wcre re- turned to Messrs. Geodeody, who declined to accept them. The duplicate of the bill of lading, held by the master, could net be altered as the vessel was at sea,and therefore the master could not es bouad by the bill of lading at all. At that stage it was agreed that when the cargo arrived it should be dealt with by the broktrs for the benefit of whom it might concorn. Die fact was that the wheat had been sold at a loss. The dispute was referred to arbiLration in Liverpool, the arbitrators be— ing Mr. Woodward for Messrs. Balfour and Williamson, and Mr. Montgomery for Messrs. Goodbody, with Mr. Paul as umpire. 'roe arbitrators were requested to state a case on a question of law, and, as they declined, a summons was taken out to prevent their making an award. The Master ordered that the matters referred to in the award, which the arbitrators had purported to have made, /Mould be remitted back to them to state a cam for the opinion of the court. The point had reference to whether Runcorn was a part of Manchester. The Vanduava could not pass ituacorn bridge without dismantling her .masts,but it was pointed out that she could go to the Runcorn lay-by, which was part of the pert of Manchester. Toe sellers appealed to Mr. Justice Bruce, who dismissed the appeal, out it was understood that toe arbitrators had power to restate their award in the form of a special case. After various steps had been taken the arbitrators eventually made an award without having given an opportunity for evidence to be heard on the point whether Runcorn was or was not a part of the port of Maucueeter. The award of the arbitrators was to the effect that they found that Man- chester was not a " safe port" for the Vanduava, aad that the documents with the eresurea as to Manchester, and which the buyers had refused to take up, substan- tially fulfilled the requirements of the contract. They awarded that these documents must be accepted by the buyers, and that Metiers. Goodbody must pay the coats. It was in respect of that award that an order was made by the master, Macdonald, sending it back for a state- ment of the facts more fully as to Manchester being a "sale port," aud as to whether Runcora was part of the port of Manchester. The arbitrators, in their further award stated that in the proceedings it was contended that if the vessel could not get to Manchester, it could have gone to EIIaCOM lay-by, in the Manchester Ship Canal,below BUDGE/nit Bridge, and that the words "Men. cheater accepted," included Runcorn. Runcorn had long been known to the commercial world as a port on the river Mersey. The award added that it was reached by going twelve miles up the canal. The effect of the award, counsel observed, was that" Mancheater accepted" in tile bill of lading,simply meant Manchester docks, and tile arbitration had U.S given Messrs. Good- body an opportunity of going into that, and showing that Runcorn was part of the port of Manchester by Act of Parliament, and warrant by a Treasury Warrant dated the 31st December, 1893. Their lordships would find,Mr.Bray added,that the ether side tried to establiah that the words" Manchester accepted" in the charter party were iramaterial,because the Vanduava could not go to the port of Manchester, and it was important to stow, therefore, that Emmen, ley.by was part of the port uf Manchester. But the arbitrators refused to hear them at all,and on that ground he submitted that the award against Messrs. Goodbody should be set aside. . . . .

j Mr. Danck worts said the arbitrators had adopted the usual course in connection with tho arbitration, and in compliance with the order of the court had stated their j award in the form of a special case, that the port of Manchester meant what was commercially known as Manchester and tnat Runcorn meant what was commer- cially known as Runcorn. The real point of this case w&s that after the wheat was bought by Messrs. Good- body the price came down with a run, and that what- ever happened, unless they could get out of the contract I on a technicality, Messrs. Goodbody were bound to lose by it. Therefore they would he satisfied with nothing I but a finding all round in their favour. The only ques- tion before the arbitrators was that as the vessel could not get past Runcom Bridge, whether she could be ordered to Runcorn lay-by, and they found that Runcorn lay-by was not commercially known as part of the port of Manchester. They further found distinctly that so far as commercial understanding went, the vessel could be easily ordered to Runcorn lay-by. The people of Liverpool were in no doubt as to what was meant by Runcorn and what was meaut by Manchester as coin. thercial ports. After considerable argument, his Lordship held that it was desirable that Messrs. Goodbody Should be heard on the point as to Runcorn being part of the port of Manchester, and eventually it was decided to refer the matter to fresh arbitrators on that issue,leaviag the rest of the award by the old arbitrators to stand.

EQUITABLE LA.ND NATIONALISATION. By JOSEPH HYDER. General Secretary of the Land Nationaliss.i.,tce Society. ARTICLE XXI. Time has ripened the doubt in the minds of some of those who were responsible for the proposals of IEB3 whether it would not have been wiser to carry this principle still fur- ther by levying an annual payment due from the tenant to the State in perpetuity, and so reserving for the Irish State a perpetual advantage from the present use of Imperial credit. That is to say, the Irish State would became the landlord, and the tenant would acquire his holding, subject to a perpetual rent of not less thus 4 per cent on the purchase money. ME. JOHN MORLET, "North Ameridan Review," October, 1893. In the execution of some scheme which displaces a large number of existing dwelliggs, it the mmucipality is to in- terfere in this matter it ought to acquire the land and retain the land for itself. It ought not to seek the creation of new interests svhleh will make sabsequent dealinga with the soil more difficult, and will put the unearned increment into the pockets of the individual. The municipality ought to acquire the land for itself, aud then I agree it becomes its duty to let it out upon reasonable terms to persons who de- sire to use it.ltr.Afiquini at Birmingham January 22ne1,189d. I think it has now been made clear that the right to compulsorily dispossess landlords upon equitable terms is well established and universally tecog,nised. There- fore land nationalusers have no need to fight for a prin- ciple. For it is conceded on all bands. .Not even the re- actionary Liberty and Property Defence League, whose president is the master of 62,000 broad acres, can deny its validity and justice. And, on the other hand, even Henry George, the apostle of confiscation, admits (vide the chapter on " Compensation" in ' The Perplexed Pnilesopher ") that it is just to compensats for land taken piecemeal for public purposes. As Mr. Balfour said in one of the debates on the Parish Councils Bill, we are all perfectly familiar with the practice and the policy of compelling the sale of land." During the same debate SirEleary Fowler told the House that, in the city of London alone, land had been compulsorily acquired under Michael Angelo Taylor's Act for the widening of streets no less than a thousand separate tiraes. SIR ROBERT T. Rano's RESOLUTION. And here I give the exact terms of a famous resolu- tion which was introduced by Sir Robert T. Reid, the eminent and respected Radical Q.C., on May 6:13, 1890 :
whol

" That in the opinion of this House a measure is earnestly needed enabling Town Councils and County Councili in England to acquire by agreement or compel- , gorily on fair terms and by simple, inexpensive maehin-1 ery,such land within or adjoining their several districts as may in their judgment be needed for the tequire- meets of the ineabitants.' Sir Robert Reid made an admirable and convincing speech which was a weighty indictment of the whole system of private property in land. Mr. A. R. Dyke Acland seconded the motion, and a long and spirited debate ensued, in the course of which Mr. John Morley strongly supported the motion as pointing to a solution of the land problem which was' reasonable, moderate, and involved no breach of equity," The whole of the Liberal members present voted for it, and they were only beaten by the Ministerialists by the narrow ma- jority of 18. The exact numbers were 185 "Noes" and 159 "Ayes." Perhaps not many of the 159 realised that tne logical outcome of the policy they eupported is the nationalisation of the land through the agency and under the administration of representative local autho- rities. Yet so it was ; and it is the policy which the Land Nationalisation Society have advocated for the last twelve years. Titus at least the first part of the process of graduality extinguishing the private owner- ship of land by the method of compensation is seen to be " practical politics." 11.0MESTZAD For let us imagine that the law was altered on the lines above suggested. And such alteration is only a question of time: it is bound to come sooner or later. Let us imagine that local Councils have the power te obtain and hold land according to the requirements et all classes ot their constituents, as was put forward in the Newcastle programme. Tne clerk, the artisan, the shopkoeper,the iermer,and the professional man ' equally : witu the labourer, would have the right to apply direct to the Council for tne land they needed. And the co- operative scciety would have as good a right as the in- dividual. Moreover, there would not be tbe absurd,and ttajust restrictions that now apply. Hitherto public bodies have only been empowered to compulsorily pur- chase land for cultivation. The utmost size of any one holding so acquired is at present one acre,an area which is not sufficient to reader a man independent of wage service. Again, there is no right to build a home on the land. The new law would remeay all this. The miser- able inadequacy of mere "potato patches " has been abundantly demonstrated. The next move must be the homestead allotment. And the establishment of the home on the land, BO that every home has its garden, is the most important use to which the land can be put. Moreover, it the price paid tor the land be a reasonable one it will be possible for the Council to compete with private land monopolists in the most effective manner, and to offer advantages which they never now give to their tenants. A fair revisable rent, and full security in the mating of improvements, are not the least of these advantages. In this way experiments in public land- ownership would be made in all parts of the country. The two systems would he seen at work side by side. They would compete for tenants. Competition would be called in to break up monopoly—competition between the public landlord, studying the public interests, and the private landlord, whose first aim is to exact the highest possible rent. Under each circumstances, given a fair trial, I do not fear for the result. The better system would win. The law of Natural Selection would operate, and the fitter (the one that better served the interests alike of the individual tenant and of the corn. =unity) would survive. Tux FINANCIAL SOUNDNISII OF COMPZNSATION. But whether the land be nationalised (under munici- pal administration) hit by bit, as fast as public opinion ripens in each district, or on a wholesale scale by a single Mt of Parliament, there arises an ebjeetien which needs to be met and answered. It mops up continually In all discussions upon the subject. It la said that it is impossible to raise the vast &Mount of money which would be needed for the purpose of buying out the land- lords. To many minds this is the pens asinorium of the whole problem. Yet the difficulty which it presents is more apparent than real. It is based in the main open two false assumptions—first, that the State must pay the landlords in cash ; second,that a vast addition would be made to the National Debt, which would have to be borne by the taxpayers of the country. Of course it is obvious that if eitner of these assumptions were correct, which j not the case, the scheme would be impracticable. As regards the objectien that the State could never find sufficient mousy, it must be remembered that the amount of actual cash in the eiruntry at soy given time is never more than a small proportion of the business done or of the liabilities which are at any given moment outstanding. If all debts incurred in the course of business had to be paid at mice, they could certainly not be paid in Cash. This is equally true of the enormous debts which have been incurred by the Imperial Government and by the vari- ous local governing bodies; debts which now exceed £800,000,000 and are constantly increasing. The whole of the metal money in the country would net be nearly sufficient to meet these liabilities alone. Yet no one says that our Government is insolvent because the available cub is less than the total liability. The Government is able to pay the interest on the National Debt every year as it becomes due. And that is the essential coeditien of solvency. Whenever the holders of Government Stock want to convert their paper into ease they can easily do so in the open market. Similarly, in national- isieg the land the State could not if it would,and would not if it could,fiad cash equal to its liability. It would issue Redeemable Land nonds,not cash. But these Bondi ' could at any time be converted into cash, just as Con- sols are. And now as regards the second objection, that the National Debt would be enormously increased. It takes no account at all of the corresponding increase whieh would be in the national assets. This is the vital point. Every argument which omits it is obviously Moan- dated. No bemuse TO THE NATIONAL DEEP. The National Debt has been incurred by war expendi- ture. But there is no comparison between money spent in that way and money spent in buy- ing land. The one is unren.unerative the other Is remunerative. However necessary a war-ship may be, it earns no money that can be placed as a set-off against its cost. That cost must inevitably be borne by the tax- payers. But suppose the same sum were employed to acquire land. Then teem would be an annual rent which would not only suffice to pay the interest on the pur- chase money but would also pay off the principal in a certain number of years. Thus, se far from there being any addition to the burden ot taxation,there would even be obtained a considerable addition to the national in- come, and coosequently a proportionate diminution of that burden.ln fact the surest way of reducing taxation is for the State to obtain its revenue from the rent of its own land, and the surest, cheapest, and justest way to Secure that property is by toe method of compensation. Tax HENT-PURCIIAsa SYSTEM AT Woao. Pontunately this is not a question of mere guesswork. The Ashbourne Acts of 1885 and 1889 and the Land Purchase Act of 1891 have shovrn that the wholesale pur- chase of laud by , the State is perfectly practicable with- out calling upon the taxpayer for a single farthing. ' Under the Althboutue Acts the interest on the sum ad- vanced is 3 per cent. The tenant pay, 4 per eent.,which is considerably lees than his former rent, and the differ- ence forms a ~king fund which pays off the principal in 49 yea„. Lien, then, we have the financial essentials of Land Natieuslieation by Compensation. Of course we know the Stare will not, after all, obtaia the land which it, has boaght. That is the absurd part of the business. It quixotically intends to hand the land over to the tenants inatead or retaining it as public preperty. But this does not alter the fact that the State has bought the land, and that the tenants' tents, even after being reduced, bave repaid the whole Of the principal. And woo is there to prevent English, and Scotch. and Welsh land being bought by the State in the same way, but retained for the good of all, instead of alienated for the benefit of a single clage ? There is no limit to the

amount of land that could be thus natio dalised. It would he as easy, ilnancially speaking, to acquire the whole 77,000,000 acres, worth (say) £3,000,000 and yielding an income of £150,000,000, as it would be to acquire a lt•sstr area. For it is a question of credit, not of cash ; and British credit would be immeasurably strengthened if the rent of the British Isles were payable to the public exchequer instead of to " Sir John or His Grace."
THEFT OF A WARRINGTON FOOTBALL PLAYER'S HANDBAG.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Wednesday morning, Thomas Blair and James Doyle, middle-aged men, were charged before Mr. John Geddes(in the chair) and Mr. Birched, with stealing a football bag, contain- ing a sweater, a cap, a pair ol boots, a jersey, a pair of pants, lee., the property of Pnilip A. Naylor, a well. known forward in the Warrington Rugby Football Club. —The Chief Constable said the prolocutor was a well- known footballer and a member of the Warrington Foot- ball Club. On tke previous slight he attended a practice on the Wilderspool ground, after which, at about 10.30, he called at the Moulders' Arms to obtain some refresh- ments. Whilst there the prisoner Blair came up to where Naylor was sitting and produced a silk handker- chief, which he asked the prosecutor to purchase. , The other prisoner took a seat near to Naylor. Shortly afterwards Naylor had occasion to leave the room and when he returned be missed the bag, the prisoners hav- ing also disappeared. He gave information to the pelice, and Detectives Meacock and Forater inquired into the matter with the result that they went to the Model Lodging House on Friars Green. Doyle was in the kit- chen, and when he was overhauled they found he was wearing a sweater, which bad been taken fro:n the bag. The initials of the club had been turned inwards so that the le%ters might not be seen. The other prisoner was upstairs in the bedroom, and upon searching him they found he was wearing the stolen pants ; in fact all the articles of clothing were recovered eccept the shinguards which had disappeared. When brought to the Police Station and formally charged, Blair said "['bat is right what you say. Did Naylor see me take the bag ?" D-. 1 le replied "I know nothing about it. i bought the sweater for gd from him" (pointing to Blair). Blair then said " You have got it off a forgeman." The bag was found at the lodging house.—Evidence in support of the above statement was given.—Blair, who is a powerfully built man,looked in a very menacing manner towards Naylor as he gave his evidence, and also conducted himself in a disorderly manner in the box. He denied that ha had stolen the bag, and Doyle said " I know nothing about the matter."—When asked by the Clerk if be had any thing to say,Blair replied "I will say what I have to say at the ether end." Doyle again asserted his innocence.— The prisoners were committed to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial.

SUCCESSFUL APPEAL BY THE CANAL COMPANY. In the Admiralty Court on Wednesday Mr. Justice Barnes delivered his reserved judgment in the case of the Manchester Ship Canal Company v. the owners of the as. Harold. The action arose out of the smashing of the Latchford Lock gates on the Ship Canal by the des fendant's steamer Harold,of Glasgow,running into them at a high rate of speed. Defendants admitted liability and paid £9,200 into court, but the p!aintiffs claimed £13,701 18s. 7d. At the reference to assess damages the registrar disallowed several of the items claimed by the plaintiffs and reduced their claim to £10,846 13s. 2d. Plaintiffs now appealed tor the full amount, and there was also a cross appeal by the defendants against many of the items allowed to the plaintiffs. The Canal Com- pany's appeal was mainly with regard to two items—the cost of the temporary new steel gates, for which they had claimed £3,470 and had been allowed only £1,735, and the cost of the removal of the intermediate gates from the lock for whica they claimed £3,118 and haa been allowed only £2,157. His Lordship said the accident, which was of a very singular character, was due to the negligence of the person in charge of the engines and resulted in very heavy damage to the plaintiffs. Taking defendant's appeal first he was of opinion that no ground was made out for reducing the amount allowed by the rsgistrar. But with respect to the plaintiff's appeal, his lordship thought that with regard to some of the items dis- allowed by the registrar they had been reasonably in- curred to avert the consequences of this extraordinary accident. He also thought the registrar was wrong in reducing the amount claimed for the temporary gates on the ground that they were a valuable asset to the plain- tiffs, who said they were perfectly useless to them now. The chances of using them again were very remote, and the plaintiffs ought to have full allowance for them. In the result his Lordship increased the £10,846 13s. 21. allowed by the registrar to £12,987 19r. 2.1., and gave plaintiffs the costs of the reference and the action.

A WARRINGTON WORKMAN'S DRUNKEN FREAK.

On Mondav morning at the Warrinitr-in-Ti;:ough relics Court, before Mr. F. Monks and a full bench of magistrates, Ar.hur Shsw, 16, Scott-at.. was charged with having stolen a silk handkerchief on Saturday afternoon from Mr. Houghton's pawnshop in Mersey-it., and also with having stolen a dress skirt from Mr. Les- lie's shop.—The Chief Constable said that on S.turday afternoon P.C. Taylor while at Warrington Bridge in plain clothes observed the defendant, wh-) was tar ad- vanced in liquor, ge up te a shop and pull some boots away. They fell to the ground and he left them there. Re then went to Mr. Houghton's shop an] looked at BOTIIO silk handkerchiefs. After examining some he picked one up and put it in his picket. He then went aeross to Mrs. Leslie's shop, took down a woman's skirt, and made off down Hall-st. The officer followed him and saw him in an entry trying to conceal the skirt. It smacked more of a drunken freak than anything else. Din man was well known as a respectable man in the town earning a very high wage. He seemed rather to nowt detection than otherwise.—Mr. Browne appeared for the defendant, and said that the man had an exeel- lent character. On Saturday he met a friend whom he bad not seen for eight years and was drinking all day. He asked their Worships to consider it more as a drunken freak than an attempt to commit a felony, and to simply record • conviction, or dismiss ths case on payment of the costs.—A fine of 10a. an I costs was im- posed in the first case, and in the ace. ,id a conviction was recordwd.

shawl, and tw-; skirts—She pleated .guilty.—The Chief Colistoble statel that a few days before the date of the theft the girl presented herself to Mr.. Peplow and asked if she wanted a servant. Mrs. Peplow, having a child six months old, engaged her for a few days. On the 7th Desember Mr. and Mrs. Peplow left her in charge of the shop, and when they returned she had gone and taken with her a shawl and two skirts belonging te Mrs. Peplow. Information wis given to the police and it was found that she had left the town. She was wearing one of the skirts, and she admitted that she had pawned the other at Jackson's pawnshop on the same day that she left the town, and she pledged the stem in Liverpool, and gave the ticket to a girl at a conamonl lodging-house there. When she MIS apprehended she first made a rambling statmsent, but afterwards admitted having stolen the articles Everything had been done to put her in " the straight way,' but evidently she preferred to go her own way. Mr. Taylor, the police court missionary, had got her into show) twice. Prisoner was sent to gaol for three months.

WYCLIFFE .P.S. A. SOCIEIY.-OPEN MEETING.

As is usual at the "open meeting" of this society there was a large attendance, the members with their wives and friends assembling in such good numbers as to fill the church. The Rev. J. Yonee, president of the 'society, was the chairman, and in the course of a few remarks he alluded to the large number of young men who appeared to be aimlessly walking the streets of the town on Sunday afternoon, and expressed the hope that the members of the P.S.A. society would endeavour to Induce some of them to enrol as members. The P was started for such as they and be was certain that it would be to their advantage to attend.—Mr. F. H. Smith, J.P , of Manchester, delivered the address For the afternoon. He referred t 3 the critical eondition of affairs In the Far East, and aloe between America and Spain. and characterised the attempt of certain newspapers to rouse UD the passions of the peoples for war as abomin- able. After alluding to the dreadful experiences of the Crimean War, and to the unheeded warnings of John Bright, the speaker said the writers who were trying to rouse the passions of the Eiglieh people were habitues of London clubs, aed unaquainted with the conditions and opinions of the working-class who felt the effects of war rnopt keenly. He advised his hearers not to be gulled by every writer in a newapiper but to judge fear- lessly and honourably for themselves. He asked them to think of the condign of many of the people in this country at the present time, and the great neei for im- provement. They needed better envirenment for the people, and increased and improved edunstilnal facili- ties. Re advised them to read good hooks, and in the home they could not spend too much time on their child• ren in educating and advising thern.—Mr. Dwell. of Wigan, sang two solos in an excellent manner, and be was also accompanied by his wife ira the duet " Love Divine." Mr.W.H. Payton presided at the organ. Mrs. William Farrar was very eueeeeeful in her recitation "The Factory Chimney " which was greatly appreci- ated. The serviee was eel taken part in by Mr. William ' Beewick, and Mr. William 13.11Widr, was an- nounced that the membership for the present year which was commenced a few Sundays ago was 835. collection was taken at the close of one of the beet meet- ings which has been held in aid of the Sec'ety's funds,

WARRINGTON "A" V. BROUGHTON RANGIIRS "A "—A fair number ef spectators gathered round the Wilder- owl Enclosure on Saturday afternoon to witness this return engrgetnent. The match will be remembered as one in which a peculiar incident occurred. The home team commenced in rare style, getting possession from every scrimmage and asserting themselves at every point of the game. To the deliaht of the spectators Jones dropped a splendid goal and everything seemed te la) going ding-dong in favour of the home team. This continued for about twenty-five minutes, and then sud- denly a temporary stoppage of the game was ordered. The visiting captain was seen to be lodging an earnest protest to the referee which for the moment,the spectators could not in the least understand. Tlae touch judges and the home captain were summ)ned to the refere-es conference, and a moment later a War- rington player was seen walking off the field. It trans- pired that the home team had been playing sixteen men. A fresh start was ordered by the referee, and the goal which was credited to Warrinron had to be taken away again. This was vexatious to a &tree, hut the specta- tors consoled themselves by the fact that they were to witness an additional half hour's play. Starting afresh the visiting forwards began to assert themselves, but aided by the wind Warrington forced their way into the visitors half, and Halcreft getting possession dropped a splendid goal for the home team, Encouraged by this suc- cess the home men played with determination, but w,re unable NA pierce the visitors'deferme.Carey got possession, and passed to Ratcliff,who punted acrops,butnothing cams of the fine opening. Ratcliffe got over a minute later, but was brought back for some informality. This was followed by another fine attempt on the part of Jones at a drop goal,which grazed the side of one of the uprights. A free kick for Broughton was charged down by An- drews and gained a little ground. An attack by the visitors took play within close proximity to the War- rineton lines, Jones falling before he could get in his kick. Carey got smartly away from a scrimmage, but foiled the effort with too strong a kick. Broughton managed to get to the line, the result of a combined rusts Iby the forwards, Jones saving just in time. When the whistle sounded for half-9m", the home team led by a dropped goal (two points) to nil. The second half was spiritedly contested, but the visit- ing forwards used their additional weight to advantage, and Thompson scored an unimproved try. A brilliant run by Rayner almost ended in eonoething tangible for the home team, hit he lied the misfortune ta slip when he had g pa sect almost all opposition. Brouhton sue- ceede-I in Filming. an additiorial try, and at the close of the Tame they ran nut winner by swo tries (six points) to Warrington one goal (two pMnti).

(1. MOUNFIELD.

Mr. Mminflald, corner of Bewsey-street, has a large stand containing a very ywied stock of hats, caps, and um- brellas. An interesting feature to visitors is the manufacture of bilk hate and umbrellas to order', sand "while you wait.' The-idea. is characteristic of Mr. Mounfteld's originality and' dqes him eredit. _

115. jonx GIiTZFITE3 AND CO. Messrs. John Gran:hilt and i/o , doh oal-street, exhibit a very attract,ve selection of Lutes blouses, juvenile blouses, and costumes, pinsfores, aprons ao., which have all been manufactured ani Aesigned on the Mtn. Two meohinsts are to be seen at work making blouses, skirts and C.

16. RALPH JouNsolf.' Mr. R Johnson, Br"dge-street, tus a large stand near the centre of the Hall where he exhibits a Sheraton bedroom suite in rich dark mahogany. There is also an oak beaureau which calls for special attention owing to its combined usefulness. Other articles shown are a boot and medicine c.mboar I. a bachelor's shaving stand, a Sheraton arm chair, and a Chippendale ;rocking chair of very graceful :design. The Hramework of the stand is enamelled white and is draped with yellow silk. The platform is covered with terra- o Atm felt.

17. HEMET)/ AM) DUTTON. The furniture exhibits by Hessrs Hesketh and Dutton, -ar key-street, comprise a five feet side-board in fumed oak ; chars upholstered in delicately shaded velvet ; one handsome chair provided with an unfixed feather cushion ; a very elegant dwarf book case with lead lights and small writing bed; and finally a splendid satin Walnut bedroom suite. The hinging, ot the stand are of satin Fr meals, and on the floor is an Indian carpet (Isllrzapore), made under the supervision of the firm by Indian prisoners. 13

T. Warm.]: AND Sox. Near one of the corridor doors, V. Virtntt'e and Son. Butter- market-street, have a fine assortment of leather belting on view, comprising single and double. link, and round belting; Helvetia hides and laces ; white hides, and laces . • walrus hide for polishing, strap butts, warranted elk bark tanned. One large pile of belting has been tanned by Messrs. W. Lang, Grappenhall. 19, MONKS, HALL, AND CO.

The imp srtant works Of Mess.rs. Monks. Hall and Co. is rep‘esented by a stand of unusually large dimensions .which contains goods frem the Be istead Department and the Tube Department. Four exceedingly handsome brass bedsteads of different patterns made at the works in School Brow, occupy one half of the stall. There is also a bechtead called the "Boss" which is a bedstead and wire mattress combined and made entirely of iron and steel. By a simple contrivance If can be stretched or relaxed at will from the outside of the bed. It can be taken apart or put together in the same time as an ordinary iron be !stead and is specially suitable for not calm ,tes as it is made exclusively from iron. An article which attr-cts universal admiration is a beautiful brass swinging cot. prettily draped. The Tube Department exhibits are a very interesting series. There are tubes from t. inch I to 6 inches in diameter, with fittings of all descriptions from Inch to 6 inches diameter ; a series of coils for heating pur- poses, refrigerators, and for blast furnaces ; a couple of wrought iron telegraph posts, and a light ladder made of tubes and which can be manufactured cheaper than wood 2. JAMES FAIRCLOUGH AND SONS. From!Mersey Mills, Msssrs. James Fairclough and Sons have stocked their stand with an interesting class of exhibits. The back of the stall is compesed of bags of flour with a huge loaf weighing 56Ibs. biked by Kr. J. Horton, as centrepiece A special show is made of Small loaves made from Fairciough's new bran meal, and a sample loaf is presented to visitors. Samples of grain from different parts of the world, aunts as English wheat wheat from Canada. the United States, Cali- fornia, Amite Video, River Plate, Russia, Turkey, India, and HgvA. are shown together with foreign peas, barley, and Indian corn. 21. lsossm RIGBY. . . _

The "Flora! Bower is one of the. best known features of the exhibitios. Miss Rigby has secured a commanding site, and her stand is of a very attractive design, and truly bower-like In appearance. The principal colours in its ornamentation are white and yellow, kl I within the enter- prising florist has a chsrming show orb oonas, table fruit, assorted fruit, and picnic;baskets. 22. ARTHUR OL A.RE. . . _ _
• Mr. A. Clare, Knutsford-road, engineer, brass founder, fte., exhibits some highly finished boiler mountings, engiue fit- tings, and a handsome brass model of a horizental eagine. W. H. PODiVoRE.

Mr. W. H. Podmore, Market Place, has an ettensive show of soortlng requisites. Everything necessary for the playing of football, cricket, tennis, &a., is displayed, the goods being all of fine quality. Stationery too has a place on the stall, and of this there is n varied assortment.

24, MERSEY CYCLE WORKS. The Warrington Syndicate Li osited,proprietors of the Mersey Cycle Works, are entitled to the high commendation their nue. cycle display woe from the visitors The stand is a capacious one and contains beautiful specimens of Budge- Whitwoe th manufacture, ton "Mersey" cycles, five Trumphs, and one Lea and Francis, a very smartly finished mschine. An exhibit which at once attracts attention is a magnificent Rudge Whitworth Quintuplet, stretching right across the front of the stand. Ladles' machines in all colours are, of course, given great preminence.

_ 25. W. H. ANT) C. LAWLEBs, This firm has shown considerable enterprise in several directions of late, and again this week in the exhibition. Stand 25 presents an alluring spectacle, loaded as it is with sweets of every kind, and tastefully draped in purple and yellow. The chief exhibits of the firm are jams, marmalade, lemon cheese, pickles, sauces, sweets, and high class confectionery. All these comestibles, it should be stated, are manufactured by the firm at their works, and every care Is taken to ensure that they shall be thoroughly pure. Particular attention is paid to the manufacture of toffee, rock, and candies. Paramount interest is however shown in the actual manufacture of all descriptions of toffee, rock and candies, during the afternoon and evening. The machinery is fixed on smo )th stone slabs, upon which the toffee is poured when bo led, and then passes through the rollers. coming out 1.1 Various shapes. It is then retailed to the eager public, and though there are ten "bolls " a day the toff Is is purchased before it has time to cool. The works of the firm are situated in Rose and Crown-street, and the retail shops at 5, Market Place, and 47, Bridge-street, 25. CIoNNAH AND BELLIAN. This firm have 16 machines on new, bassinette, mail-cart, and motor tricycle. The latter is a fine machine which has taken the a.•.* I,4ve in the Liverpool Bxhibition, and is valued at 70 guineas. The bicycles include Raleigh,. Swifts, Royal Brifields, Royal Cambrisns, (those latter the speciality of Messrs, Connah and Bellian), Rothwells, and Calcotts 27. T. DAINTITII. A combined display of cycles, cycle ascessorles. and fire- arms is made by Hr. T. Daintith, of Bridge-street, whose stall is set out to the bsst advantage. Imperial Rovers, Centaurs, Ariets, Monopoles, was among the cycles exhi- bited, and tie stock of guns, rifles, and revolvers, is a large one. The air of excellence and " class" which Mr. Dsintith's exhibits all bear has already secured him numerous orders. 30. 3.11. JORDAN. - -

Mr. S. H. Jordan, 135 Bridge-street, presents an attractive . stall to the publics, containing pictures, frames, mouldings, and pictures. Tne selections of mouldings and frames is an exceptionally good one and enxbrsc•s the latest designs and 11Patterns. all of which do the exhibitor Infinite credit. He lhas a superior line In photogravures and engravings, many 'of which are coloured. and some date back as far as lal7. Both new and old are picturei7ol,i :high quality and work- manship. . 31. • T. MIMES. • Photography is represented by a eouple.of handsome show cases containing some high-class cabinets, and enlarged photographs by Mr. T. Wrtles, Sankey-stre-t. Many of these are coloured, and the whole display is an artistic one, em- bracing !some of the best iamnies of the photographer's art. 32. MACKIE IND CO., LIMITED. Prom the works of the" Warrington Guardian " Mee was exhibited an extensive collection of commercial stationary. A bookbinder at work in the stall attracted mulls attention. 33. SUNRISE PUBLISHING COMPANY. A peculiar Interest attaches to the stand of the Sunrise Publishing Company, which consists of a large case of old Warrington literature, and book-plates, autographs and M.S.S., lent by Mr. H S. Page. and some framed pictures of the Suarlse Jubilee edition. Councillor A. Bennett has got un this exhibition for the sole purpose of familiarising the Warrington people with the Literary and Academical Associa- tions of the old town, which have been allowed to sink too much In the backgrouad. It would be impossible to particularise all the interesting contents of the case, but some of the more Imp Ttant we may mention. There is a volume of Alfred" by John Titchett. the longest poem in the English language. " Memories of th-s Bard of Warren and Surrey." which work is accounted to be one et the finest specimens of typography in its day, and was considered tO be the masterpiece of William Byres, a noted early Warrington printer. John Howard's book on •* The State of Prison.," has special interest because the author came purposely to Warrington to superintend Its production by William yres. An interesting comparison between past and present is afforded by is couple of books, one being a recent production by Mr. John Lane, one of the leading and most up-to-date publishers in London, and the other published by William ' Byres, in 1772. In the lapse of a century and a quarter the ' local production can quite hold Its own, and the similarity between the two Is remarkable Another book, 11 A Key to Southport," by T. K. Glazebrook of Warrington, published in 1809, is u .Ique from thereat that it predicts the invention of. the phonograph with astonishing accuracy. There is also a presentation copy of Dr. Priestley's "Chart of Biography." a photograph Is shown too of the Warrington window In Manchester College, Oxford, whicn contains beneath it, the inscription "What Oxford thinks of the Academy." She by side with this are photographs of the original academy hidden behind the recently demolished shoo at Bridge foot, and of the Students Quarters in Academy-street, wh‘ch has been sold as builders material. These have beneath them the In scrlption " What Warrington thinks of the Academy.' Among the autographs shown are those of Richard Le Gall- tonne. Marie Corelli, Eric Mackay, Alfred Austin. and Prin- cipal Drummond, of Manchester College, Oxford. 34, J. CEONLEY. A very nharacteristic and representative stand is that of Mr. J. Chnrley, Buttermarket-street, which consists of iron throughout, is from top to bottom rather unique. The regniations of the exhibition stipulate tht all stands must be raised 6 inches from the floor, and Mr. C honey has obeyed this behest by; making a platform of galvanised and corrugated iron sheets, laid on horse-nail boxes. Pour wrought Iron unbreakable spilt pulleys. 2 feet 6 che in diameter, re9t on thls platform and support two steel joists. The cross bearers are formed a livht bridge rails On the top lea cold-straightened steel bar 81t by 41n. The stand displays shafting, pulleys, hangers, and different sections and fractures rf iron to show the quality of the metal. Between the pulleys are shown several patterns of wrought iron rail-heads to- fencing, these being meth superior to castings. The frame bearing the name of the firm is made ef twisted wrought iron work, They are agents tar the Unbreakable Pulley Co. and Messrs. Pearson and Knowles.

_ 35. MREPIRS. ROBERTS AND SON . Messrs. R. Roberts and Son, 19. Bridge-street. make the only display of Boots and Shoes in the Exhibition and its cert dniv is well worthy of inspration. 'I he established reputation of the firm for High Class Goods is fully main- tained by this exhibit. The goods are of the Clorkaest description and Include samples of blacks' Patent, Ventilated Boots, specially recommended by the Wedlcal Journals and Physicians, as being a safeguard again. t Pulmonary and Chest Complaints. The ColebrAted X toots and shoes for which Roberts and Sort, are, Sole Local Agents, are a speciality, perfect In tit.made Of the best materials and work- manship, and quality absolutely guaranteed. The makers of these goods enjoy a reputation In the Trade which is second to none. There Is also included a very charming display of " Queen" boots and shoes as made for H.E H. the Princess of Wales, and which have been pronounced by the Trade , Journal to bathe finest specimens of combined workmanship, and the nearest approach to perfection yet seen. Golf Boots lCycling Shoat, Tennis Shoes. era also included, snit

altogether combine to make an Exhibit which reflects great 1 Credit upon the proprietors. 3L ArserreeoX The stall occupied by Mr. James Atkinson of 7, 11 and 13 Bridge-street. is in itself art exhibit of good taste. The wood- work is painted and draped with apple green, and rose pink slikette lighted by electric lights and forms a very pleasing picture. The back of the stall and one end draped in the well-known " Louis" Velveteen (2) different shades) I Is very attractive, while the costumes exhibited which have been designed and made in Mr Atkinson's own vrorkrooms speak well of the dressmakers' skill. Here is a handsome electric blue covert coat costume, lined silk and trimmed moire silk and ereme and gold elik braiding. Another cos- tume shown, is the newest style in coats and skirts in heaver cloth, lined silk.& girl's figure with wax head and hands, on which is shown a girls costume in petuna shade of" Louis " velveteen, is very tasteful, with hat to match. Under a glass case is shown a copy& a Parisian model bonnet, whia t is a revelation of the millinery art also a very handsome model hat, A novelty in sunshades is also shown in the new Vice- verse sunshades:in goffered chiffon. Taken all through, es- pecially from a ladies point of viewthis stall forms one of the most attractive in the exhibition and should not on any account be missed by visitors. 37 THE FINTII CO., LIMITED. The Firth Co., Limited, Florence Mills, exhibit wire for mattresses, superior tinned and galvanised; copper spring wire for upholsterers springs, tinned bottling wire, and all varieties of bright, tinned, and galvanised wire suitable for various purposes. They also have an excellent show of their woven wire mattresses and combination beds. Asa.. for which they are well known throughout the country and abroad ; very reliable asylum bed. constructed of ash, neatly polished with wire mattress att.ched. They have, in addition a vagrant bed, several combination and folding metallic beds of very reliable workmanship together with a variety of thatr noted woven wire and chain spring mattresses, Ice. Another development of the wire industry is the flexible wire door mats, which are strong and durable. There are also samples of wire cloth for window blinis, flour screening, stamp bat' tery careening, se-ving, lamp and joint gauze. & n., wire eon veying belts, colliery screens, sand screens, Ac,

_ 3B. _ E. N. I{E.ssroaaug IND CO. Another interesting exhibit Is that of Messrs. lienworthy and Co. Washita' Machine Manufacturer', Oldham. This firm is one of the most successful in their own particular line (3' business, and have carried off some of the very highees, awards. o,ie of the most ing snlous exhibits is the ' Handy ' Curtain Stretcher, Clothes Dryer, and Draught Screen combined. Altqgethor it appears t) be a valuable and useful invention. Other specialties arc the P tragon washing machine, the Equipoise wrin.or and mangier, and the Canadian wasloer. All hove merits out of the c,narnon and are worth the closest Inspection• 39, THE BLICEENS DERTER TYPEWRITER CO.

One of the most interesting exhibits,to commercial men especial y, is the " Blick " typwriter. This wonderful machine is not an improvement on any model of type- writers, It is an evolution in typewriter mechanism. The inventor has succeeded in doing away with the chief rearing fact le found in older makes of typewriters, and by simple inventions, puts npon the market a typewriter which can do all that the most °sperm ve machines can do and much that is impo.sible to them, at jut one third the cost. The chief point in the " Buck" are simplicity of mechanism, making it the most durable tvp writer in the market; direct inking and printing. The most speely• machine, visible writing; porta-dlity, cheapness. Amon.r users of the flick in Liverpool are the names of The Corporation, Corporation of Birkenhead, The American Line, Bawer Line. Elder Dempster and Co.. The Liverpool London and Globe, Insuruoce Co., The Bridgewater Trustees. and scores of other wel-known firms. The BLACK has taken tke highest award ever given to Typewriters. The Liverpo )1 address of the firm is, 67. Lord-street Liverpool. 40 B WHITEHoun. B. . . . .

The only tobacconist exhibiting is B. Whiteboue, 90. Bridge-street, who had a smart looking stall, well stocked with goods, in the west corridor. All kinds of tobacco, Cigarettes, Havana, Mexican, and British cigars are to be had.while pipes and fancy goods possess the additional attraction of special low prices. Stand 40 has been well pdronised during the last three days, and may expect to he las long as the exhibition remains opera.

, 1. JOSEPH OIio9FIELD LID SON& LIMITED. The place of honour as first on the list of exhibits falls to titeretrossrs. BtekPQh fary°.sti'Tillelarnedtallo.nstOoL,lnaisitepderhalli: tmh‘enumr7s; artistic and ate no lye of any. They make a spooled feature of the tint that they Ara high-oless toilet soap manufacturers, a branch of the trade only lately entered into. Toe prinalpal of the soap, the firm are making Is the Brastalo Series, a tastefully coloured and scented production which is very popular. The stall Is got up in a style eepresenting the colour of the soap and the get-up of the boxes In which It is sold. Yellow. parole and greets are principal shades, all being beautifully blended in the draping. of the framework. At the back of the stall is an enlarged edition of the firm's show-card, entit'ed " He loves me, which is worthy the ad- miration it excites Soap in the process of manufacture is shown with a reduced working model of the actual large machines used in the manufacture of Brasnaio Soap. Milling machines are used te give the soap a more subtle perfume than was possible under the. old proem of bailing. Bach day the soap Will bia_ nitenufaicturega_stampek boxed, and sold ta the public while they wait. 2. JOHN iteCLES. • The firm of John Eccles. S'alcan Work,. John-street, War- rington, have on view all kinds of weighing machines, and wire-testers. Included among the machines is an i• pectar's sensitive test Seale for testing wit:tights, And Which has been manufactured for the Madras Railway. . . 3. square yards. They are manufaoturers of - Tag tioPE FoDSDRY. ClD.slastreED. The Bova Foundry p Limited. Hallam-lane has been established about three years, their works standing on 'an area of 8 artistic aciooo uare d general castings, their specialities being Ranges. Mantel. and Registers, which are produced in various finishes, including electro-plating and enamelling in imita- tion of woods and marble. On entering the works, which have recently been entarge t . one visits the pattern shop. where the operatives with most delicate instruments are modelling the designs in clay ware, plaster, wood and tin I these whan competed are passed to a specialist in moulding with the view to testing the practicability of the designs ; and if found to be workable, are sent to the foundry to undergo the process of moulding and casting. Before reach- ing ths foundry one encounters a huge cupola belching forth large volumes of fire, and emitting every hue of the rainbow. Safely in the foundry the cast has commenced. and large vessels called bogies containing the molten metal are taken along on rails; these are discharged into smaller vessels which the men and boys carry to the boxes deposit- ing the contents into the moulds. Passing from the foundry one reaches the " dressing shop " whets the castings are denuded of any asp, rities, subsequently to pass the ordeal of the casting up shoo" where every easting,striall and large, is subjected to the test of soundness, perfection and weight ; any castings not reething the standard are rejected, broken up and cast into the furnace. Arriving at the fitting shop 011f1 encounters gigantic wheels, spinning round at enormous speed. The parts of the ranges, dro., are here brightened by the stone and emery wheels, and then handed te the fitters to be drilled and put together. In the enamelling shop the better class ot goals are finitherl in imitation of woods and marbles, the articles being given several °oats of paint and ; then placed into specially constructed stoves, by means of which the enamel is permanently deed. Haltering the electro- plating shop one finds parts of ranges, bicycles and orna- ments either in process of plating or completed, this being done by electricity. In the warehoute are stored away for immediate despatoh every kind of municipal and sanitary castings, builders' requisites, ranges, grates, gas stoves. itc. A Mantel and Mirror combined, double shelf: enamelled in light oak A Best Finished Mantel, en- amelled in three shades of green, majolica tiles, surrounding a Dawn gas the ; parlour mantel with mirror topped by a spread eagle, enamelled Italian and American walnut, tiled grate and orstanaental fender. Britannia Restaurant Table. with Sicilian marble toe, enamelled in walnut and gold leaf. An oblong Restaurant Table with mahogany top, enamelled in antique bronze. A pillar Restaurant Table with Sicilian merbie top, enamelled in cream and gold. CLAIM BY AN EMPLOYEE AGAINST
THE C.L.C.

At the Warrington County Court, last Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes,the claim for .£3 12s. which Henry Jackson,Welliagton-street, Warrington, brought against the Cheshire Lines Committee for , alleged wrongful suspension and dismissal on November 15,was resumed. Mr.Thonias‘ Swift (instructed by Messrs. Swift and Garner, St. Helens), was for the plaintiff, and Mr. Jordan (in- structed by Mr. Lingard, of Manchester) appeared for the defendant. The Case for the plaintiff was closed at the first hearing. Mr. Jordan said that no doubt his Honour would thoroughly appreciate one fact, and that was that the Railway Company attached much importance to the case,notwithstandieg that the amount claimed was only a small ose. The case set up by Jackson was one of the most extraordinary which it had been his lot to listen to. It seemed to be set out by Mr. Swift that although workmen were engaged under certain rules and condi- tions,they claimed the right to deede for themselves whether they would go or absent themselves when there was any night work to do. If such a proposition were adopted, it would be impossible for an employer of labour to carry on his work,and the result would be dis- astrous not only to the employer himself ,but a'so to the public at large. The Railway Company had important work to be done,and it was imperative that it should he done at a particular time, and that was in the night time when the traffic was not so busy as in the day time. The man Jackson had several times broken the rules,and had been fined, and at length the Company thought that they had given him sufficient opportunith 8 and dismissed him. It was prepestereus that the claim of the plaintiff should be allowed. Unless he could give valid r eason,lie was compelled to attend to his work, or he rendered himself liable to dismissal. Christopher Bowers, inspector of masonry in the em- ploy of the defendant Company,Warrington, said he was engaged in doing certain repairs along with Inspector Jane to a bridge which carried the Cheshire Linos over the London and North-Western line. It was very impor- tant wotk, and the orders were that it should be done at the week end. It was the rule to put a notice up at the office when men were required at a week end. The name of each particular man was inserted on the list,and this was known to every emplos 6. It specified the time and the place where the men should work at. If a man whose name was on the list did not• attend to his work, he would be report ed.lt was not true that it wee entirely optional fer a man to go to work or not as he chose. The man was posted to work on October 30th, and he came three hours late, between three and four o'clock in the morning. There was some work to be done before be got there. On the following week end he did not turn up in time, and his check was "turned "and another man taken on in his place. He had failed several times to come en Sunday, and he was censured for it. A copy of the rules was posted up in a frame in the mess ro. m. William Wright, clerk on the Railway, stated that he heard Jackson gay that he had never received a book of the rules, but that was not so, as every man received a ' book, and in February, 1896, Jackson came and asked for the one and witness gave him one. He also handed a declaration form signed by himself. William George Scott, engineer and inspector, said that any reports of misconduct of employes always came to him, and it lay with him to deal with the cases. Upon a report being sent to him, he dismissed Jack- On. His Honour thought it was unreasonable to consider that it was optional for men on the railway to go or not, as suppose an accident occurred during the night, and the men refused to attend to it, it would step all traffic. That was incidental work which they were called upon to do, by the nature of their work. If the plaintiff could not be relied upon, very: serious conse- quences might follow. He would give judgment for the defendants with costs.

div.head: ALLEGED BREACIT OF WARRANTY 1N THE SALE OF A COW.
div.p: ALLEGED BREACIT OF WARRANTY 1N THE SALE OF A COW.

A claim was heard at the Warrington County Court last Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, iii which Stephen Dean, farmer,Orford, sued Michael Short for £5 IN. for damages alleged to have been sustained by the breach of warranty in connection with the pur- chase of a cow. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles) for the defendant. Stephen Dean, farmer, residing atThe Poplars, Orford, where he bad carried on practice for 10 years, said : On November 15th last he was present at the Norton Arms weekly cattle sale, and was looking at a cow when de- fendant came to him. The defendant said that he had get another cow to sell. He said he had bought the cow for £8 59., and she would have a calf a fortnight after Christmas Day, and he thought she was worth £ll. Witness had some discussion, during which d4endant said that be could guarantee the time for her to have a calf, and promised to send him a paper to that effection the following day, but he had never received any. The cow was purchased for £lO. Shortly before Christmas witness suspected she was not in calf, and kept her past the 7th January, which was the time stated, and found she was not. Eventually she was sold for £l2 8s at a sale at the Norton Arms. In consequence of finding her a barren cow, a letter was sent to defendant but no re- ply was received,and the present preceedings were com- menced. If the cew had calved in January she would have been worth £l6, not taking into account the value of the calf. He had her fed up tcr butchering purposes, and charged a is a day for 38 days. James ....ongshaw Fryer. farmer, Crossing Farm, Pad. gate, stated that he was present at the sale at the Nor- ton Arms on November 15th. Before the cow was sold to Dean it was offered to him, and defendant said that she would calve a fortnight after Christmas. Be also made the same statement to defendant when he sold it to him. Henry Tipping, 30 Atberton-st., said that he did odd jobs at the Norton Arms Yard, and he attended the sales every Monday. He was present when the cow was bought and corroborated the statements of the other witnesses. ' James Brookes said he examined the oow on Fotruary 3, and found no trace of a calf. Ernest Bennett, farmer, also examined the cow on February 12, and gave evidence to the same effect. Mr. Swift said that his client emphatically denied warranting the cow, and the defendant gave evidence to that effect.
Hie Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff.
UNITED RAILWIY :TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.

CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. Wycliffe Halliwaa well filled on Thunday last week, when a concert was given under the auspices of the local London and North-Western Branch of the above association. The object of the venture was to aid the funds of the Warrington branch, which is doing a good and useful work am ong the railway men, and it is satisfactory to state at the outset that the SUM of about ..£l2 profit was realised. The audience included the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. J. l. Wright), Councillor and Mrs. H. Roberts, Councillor Smethurst, Alderman Francomb, Mr. and Mrs. Neald, Mr. and Mrs. Weide. Dr. and Mrs. Braide, Mr. and Mrs. Page (Earlestown), Mr. W. J. Forshaw Mr. E. Smith, Mr, T. Shentee, and Mr. R. Wood. A attractive programme was sustained by the following artistcs:—Mrs. Barr,soprano (Bolton); Mrs. Alfred Dear. den, elocutionist (Bolton) ; Mr. Flowerdew, bass (Man- chester); Mr. Horton, instrumentalist (Manchester); Mr. J. Davenport. tenor (Warrington) ; Mr. F. L. Scott, humorist (Runcori3); and Mr: W. J. Bell,humorist (War• ington. The items were received with much enthusiasm and the evident enjoyment of the audience testified to the success of the concert. Mrs. Dearden is a most cap- , able elccutionist and her expressive and feeling recitals of " Not one to spare," "Domestic Asides," etc.,won her unstinted applause and a couple of encores. A cordial reception was given to Mrs. Barr,whe however was not so successful in her song " May Morn," as in " Zanita." for which she was deservedly recalled, and gave the pretty and amusing song" Do as they do in France." A good bass was found in Mr. Flowerdew whose render- ing of "Soldiers of the Queen," and " Will o-th-Wisp " was hearty, spirited and tasteful. Mr. .1. Davenport sang skillfully in "Queen of the earth "and "Good COM- panv,"both being warmly applauded. Ad a humorous singer Mr. Scott, though he greatly amused his hearers, was rather flat. His Irish selections were his best and most praiseworthy efforts. The parts allotted to Mr. Horton made a great " hit." His musical instru- ment was nothing but a mouth-organ, and apart from the uniqueness of the performance, the skill and har- mony he evoked were marvellous. No less than three Encores were insisted upon, " Belphegor," " Killarney." and an imitation of a bugle band being Mr. Horton's responses. Hearty amusement was afforded by Mr. W. J. Bell, who in his sketch " House Painting," and imi- ations of the phonograph, bag pies, &c., was an unfail - log source of homour.—Mr. Hardman (Manchest-r) accompanied the artistes efficiently. Three cheers for the )tayor and Mayoress bought an ei:j )yable contest to a close.

div.p: Lettero to tbe ebttor.
iTO-1-si HKA'n

sir,—We in Stockton Heath at an—y--;;;;—c;anot com- plain like the inhabitants of some places in tiae neigh- bourhood of a dearth of aspirants who are anxious to represent, and guard our interests, in the matter of parochial government. As one who did not attend the parish meeting,let me say that I thoroughly approve the action of the gentlemen who demanded a pall; as count- ing hands at an excited public meeting cannot be con- sidered a satisfactory way of taking the opinion of the whole of the ratepayers. Like others I have received the famous batch of seven addresses in one envelope. The one conspicuous feature in each address is the utter absence of a policy, except to express their indiguation that a poll was to be taken,and a lame attempt to make capital out of the trifling expense incurred, which no one is concerned about. These dear gentlemen are much exercised about putting the smallest extra burden on the ratepayerstas such gentlemen always are when an;- lig for votes. This concert of seven reminds one of the famous con- cert of the great powers of Europe, to deal with tbe unspeakable Turk. The poor Armenians and Cre- tans will curse the memory of that concert down to the latest period of time. Let us hope this will not prove to be our experience if this concert of seven is found to be triumphaat at the declaration of the poll. The rate- payers have only to read these addresses, an I those of Messrs. Mason, England, Pemberton, and Welsby, to know who are likely to best represent them. For one thing this contest will be memorable. It has by sone law or process which I cannot define evolved, or developed, a local genius for writing twaddle. In one of your contemporaries appear contain notes, and per. I hap s in the history of journalistic literature it would be difficult to find the counterpart of twaddle so absolutely pointless and meaningless.—Yours, &c., HUSTICI:B. Stockton Heath, March 31st, 1193.

div.head: NN 'BENING OF BRIDGE-STREET.
div.p: NN 'BENING OF BRIDGE-STREET.

Sir,—Mr. Councillor Henry Roberts, the chairman of the Property Purchasing Sub-Committee, has became notorious for allowing his ar parentiy ungovernable temper to get the better of hi, judgment whenever he is thwarted in his attempts to have everything his own way. He has been accustomed to be so pampered and indulged by his own political party that now he finds his influence is on the wane, owing to a spirit of independence recently manifested by some who abso- lutely refuse to submit to his autocratic rule, he cannot contain himself or refrain from persistently snarling and snapping at everyone who dar-s to oppose his views. So far as the charges Mr. rloberts makes against myself in his indiscreet letter' the local news- papers last Saturday (and why he nakes me a mark for all his bitterness I don't understa, ad), they do not trouble me in the least, as I have a clear conscience in respect to everything which relates to personal interests in connection with the Corporation.lf Insmotive is to try to convince the public that lam unworthy of their confi- dence as an alderman of the borough in taking advantage of any private knowledge I possess as Chairman of the Street Improvement Committee, and in divulging that knowledge in the present arbitration for the purpose of furthering my own interests, then it must be obvious to everybody, and especially to himself, that be is acting unjustly, because it will be well known that for several months past I have incurred Mr.Roberts7 displeasure by strenuously opposing arbitration, and have continually complained that both the Street Improvement Commit- tee and the Town Council have been ignored and snubbed by the Property Purchasing Sub-Committee in their stubborn refusal for a period of three or four years to afford UR the slightest information as to what was being done in regard to the widening of Bridge-st., or to make any attempt to settle the case without resort to arbitration ; and further that all the information I afforded at the arbitration inquiry was nothing more than what the solici- tors and all the other local witnesses had pre- viously obtained for themselves from the public news- papers. If Mr. Roberts' presumption carries him so far as to contend that I have no right,whenever disagreeing with the action of any committee of the Corporation, to defend the interests of any individual ratepayer or body of ratepayers who, I believe, are being untairly and un- justly treated, or that I should first obtain his sancticn as to the way I should conduct my own private business then I say such ridiculous notions are only on a par with the rest of his absurd ideas. I again repeat that Mr. Roberts is the very last man who sliluld talk about personal interests,and it would be far mere interesting to the public if, instead of continually harping on this subject and attacking everybody else. he would tell them how much his own firm (of which he is the managing director), and in which he is the largest shareholder, derives an- nually from their contracts with the Corporation. The Jaw which allows his firm, but denies the privilege to the members of a Corporation not connected with a limited liability company to accept work from that Cor- poration, is to me very one-sided, and the sooner the law is altered the better. I must apologize for troubling you with so long a letter, but when my honour and honesty are attacked, I am not justified in tamely submitting to It. I have always been ready to admit that Mr. Roberts's abilities, if rightly applied, are of no common order, and it he would only be more considerate and less dictatorial and abusive he would have the support of, yours, Zco.,
THOMAS H. soTroN.
