When the war cloud burst over Greece, net about a year ago, there were many who beheld in that unhappy event the prelude to a Europe,an Arma- geddon. To-day the portents are even more men- acing. For the time being, it is true, the greater nations of the earth are at peace. At all events. they are not engaged iu actual war. But at any moment, as everyone feels, the loose gunpowder that is lying about in so many parts of the world may catch fire, and involve us in a general con- flagration. A week ago it looked as if the first spark might be kindled in the Far East. At the present moment all eyes are turned to the West, for it is realised now that the danger is far more im- minent in that quarter than it has yet been in the region of the Yellow Sea.

The:death,by her own hand,of the daughter ()Iliad Marx,Mrs.Eleanor Marx Aveling—as she was usually called—is a very sad event, Eleanor Marx was for many years a notable Agure in the English Social- ist movement. She inherited something of her father's rhetorical and analytical genius, and she was one of the best women speakers—on her own subjects, perhaps the best—we have ever heard. She spoke an easy, pure, and idiomatic English, at once correct and strong,and as an open air orator,in Myde Park and elsewhere, she had some notable successes. /ler strong,clear,vibrant voice,a certain passion of manner, a little hard, perhaps, and a faculty for the clear presentment of economic rea- soning, showed a remarkable personality and a talent which, had it been a little more nicely de- veloped,would have led her far. She was full of life and energy, spoke and wrote English, French, and German equally well, and if she had chosen some more popular cause than Socialism, might have made a lasting mark on her time.

The Tichborne Claimant was quite a grand gentle- man at one time when his backers lent him money freely,and the Tichborne bonds were at a premium. He was a good shot at pigeons, and was a great frequenter of the Gun Club. Curiously enough, the present it Henry Tichborne is also very nimble at the traps. The claimant, by the aid of Lord Rivers and Mr. Guildford Onslow, was elected to a West- end club, where he somewhat astonished the mem- bers on election by sending round the water to ask everybody indiscriminately what they would have to drink, which is hardly an uppenclass custom. Tichborne Park, which was then in dispute, is beautifully situated among the Hampshire downs where the Itchin rises, but the house is nothing to look at and of modest proportions. Inside are por- traits of Roger Tichborne's mother, who recognised the Claimant as her son and who must have been a beautiful woman, and of Roger Tich borne himself as a very foreign-looking young man. It is curious that several officers of the Carabiniers, in which the real Tichborne served,swore to the Claimant as their old brother officer. This was largely owing to the fact that Roger Tichborne's servant was an ally of the Claimant.

The Duke of Newcastle has been the means of producing a new protest against ritualism. By way of retaliating upon certain Low Churchmen, the Duke offered to give censers to six of the poorer London churches on conditions that they should be used at all choral celebrations. As a retort the Low church and Evangelical Associations are taking steps to lodge formal protests at the Easter vestry meetings of those parishes in which ritualistic practices are followed against all" Popish metnods and idolatries." They have issued instructions as to the form which the formal notice to the rector and churchwardens should take, and I hear that protests may be looked for in at mast sixty or seventy parishes in London and neighbourhood.

Relics of the Benin expedition are apparently in- exhaustible. The last lot sold in a London auction- room were notable chiefly for their ghastly associa- tions. At a further sale this week more than one of the articles brought under the hammer had some artistic pretensions. The ex-King's mace, which was discovered in the "palaver house,"where it had been left when the King and his people fled at the approach of the English force, realised about ..£4O. A piece of exquisite ivory carving, in the form of a mask surmounted by Italian coral beads, sold for ..£2O ;while • number of brass and bronze ornaments, some of them very antique, realised prices ranging from 7 to 13 guineas.

The Prisons Bill, after a debate lasting several hours, passed its second reading without a division in the House of Commons on Monday evening. The two most striking speeches of the evening were made by Mr. T. P. O'Connor, who spoke from ob- servation, and Mr. John Burns, who spke from experience. It is a remarkable fact, indeed, that throughout the discussion on this bill member after member has been able to command particular atten- tion to his arguments by proclaiming himself, amid the hushed respect of his colleagues, an old political gaol-bird who knew what he was talking about. Mr. Burn's autobiographical memories were very painful, and gave a keen edge to his remarks. For example, the Home Secretary, in intimating his willingness to make further inquiry into the dietary regulations of her Majesty's prisons, had ' pointed with some bewilderment to his official statistics, showing that prisoners often increase their weight whilst in gaol. "Try a day or two in Pentonville yourself," Mr. Burns argued, " you will agree with me that the diet Metilli starvation." Sir Matthew, thinking of his other engagements, de- clined the invitation.

There has been perhaps more scattering of the Royal Family this year than ever before. The Duke of York has been fly fishing en garcon on Deeside, while the Duchess of York is in the South of France attended by her lady-in-waiting. The Prince of Wales is cruising in a hired yacht, the Princess of Wales travelled alone to Copenhagen, and the Prin- cess Victoria arrived on Saturday at Cromer, who're she will enjoy the undivided occupation of a villa enga ,ed tor the purpose. The separation of the family of the Prince of Wales in this way is the more remarkable because of the habits fos:ered during many years by her Royal Highness, as a result of Which the Princess of Wales wai seldom unaccompanied by one or more of her children, and it is this long training that enables them nowadays to take up with confidence their individual lives.

Mr. flanbury's concession of a Select Oommittee to inquire into the desirability of granting tele- phone licenses to municipalities has created much satisfaction in commercial circled, though it it is as a very cautious sod timid one if tis taken seriou i sly. On the other hand, tis merely a device for letting the National Tefephone.Conopany gently down. It is much too considerate, to face of his own acknowledgment that the company. byin- vading Government areas, has beaten the Govern- ment out of the field. It is worth noting, however, that the inquiry as defined by Mr. fianbury is not 9neinto the efficiency of the service at present ex- isting. it takes the efficiency and costliness for I granted, so that it will be impossible to protract the inquiry by a long investigation into the merits of the compsny's service. The points that will go before the committee do not even give the coin- panv a locus stand'. They are simply the prudence of allowing corporations to start a telephone service out of the rates, and of allowing them to conduct business to some extent outside their own areas. To both there can only be one answar, and neither requires much labonr or many witnesses. Jhe committee ought to report by Whitsuntide, and a 1 Bill should be =through Parliament immediately afterwards.

For the first time on its preseat cruise the Chan- nel squadron is able to show a clean bill of health, and it is to be hopea that the last has been seen of the measles epidemic, which kept breaking out so mysteriously. The admiral is keeping everyone very busy, and the squadron is working at the highest:pressure. What with coaling, which was done the other day in exceedingly good time, and steam tactics, everyone has been hard at it.

Contests took place in four wards of the Borough on Monday for seats on the Warrington Board of Guardians. There are nine representatives for War- rington on the Board but five of these were returned unopposed, viz: Mrs. Clay, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, William Ilickman,S.Davies,and T.H. Ashcroft. The candidates in the contested wards were as follow : Orford Ward (1099 electors) Mrs. Edeleten, 31,Bold- street, and Mr. William James Shaw, 89, Dallam- lane, builder; St. John's Ward, (1606 electors), Mr. James Battersby, 22, Cartwright-street, filesmith, and the Rev. William Hamilton Drummond, 20. It cannot ba said that very much interest was aroused in the various contests. The only ward in which the candidates may be said to have fought in downright earnest was in St. John's Ward. This ward was previously rearesented by a Trades Coun- cil nominee—Mr. A. Lang—and on his retire- ment the Trades Council nominated Mr. James Bat- tersby. The Rev. W. H. Drummond entered the lists against him, and as will be seen from the figures below, succeeded in heading the poll. Mr. W. J. Shaw was the retiring candidate in Orford Ward, and was opposed by Mrs. 3. Neither in Orford nor Latchford does Mr. Shaw appear to have re- ceived the support of the ratepayers, being deci- sively defeated in both places. In Fairfield Ward, Mr. Pilling, the Chairman of the Board and of the Assessment Committee, was opposed by Dr. McCarthy, and the chief point brought out during this contest has been the assess- ment of Warrington, more particularly with refer- ence to public-houses. div.head: HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The 18th annual report of the Medical Officer of Health for the Borough of Warrington (Dr. J. H. Gornall) has Just been issued and contains as usual a good deal of in- teresting information with regard to the borough. Dr. Gornall says in hi' introductory remarks that : " The year was an eventful one in the history of War- rington,the burgesses entering into full possession of an extended borough,defined by a Provisional Order of the Local Government Board,lB9B, which actually came into operation at the municipal election of that yi ar. The event was celebrated by a fife day on the 3rd April, commemorative of the Jubilee of the Corporation. On that occasion two important open spaces were preserved to the town ,one to he known as ' The Queen's Gardens,' situated in the centre of the town,and having an area of nearly 5,000 square yards ; the other situated In the more rural portion of the borough, viz., Latchford,and, in the words of the Mayor, ' declared that a portion of the estate (the area of which will be subsequently de- fined) is hereby dedicated to the inhabitants of the borough of Warrington to be for ever used by them as a public park, and to be known by the name of • The Victoria Park,' in commemoration of the 50th anni ver- s.:lry of the incorporation of the borough and of the long reign of her most gracious Majesty Queen Victoria." _

div.head: STATE OF TRADE:
div.p: STATE OF TRADE:

1 Dr. GORNALL rep 3rte-t-ba-t-heiTaireceived the follow- ing opinions bearing on the state of trade and manufac- tures in the Borough during the year 1897 : " law kiateurecruins, kc.—Altbough there was a considerable improvement in the iron and steel trades during the late autumn of 1896, the revival was arrested before the beginning of 1897, chiefly as a result of the famine and plague in India and of political and commer- cial disturbance in Eastern Europe and in other parts of the world. During the latter part of 1897, however, there has been a slight improvement, with a better demand for iron and steel. This has enabled manufac- turers to keep their works more fully employed, and the outlook for 1898 is a little brighter." "TANNING.—AS far as the Tanning Trade is concerned the past year has been one of considerable tension. The unnatural boom that occurred in the autumn of 1895 has been felt very adversely during the whole of the year. The depression resulting from this cause has been in- creased by the Engineers' strike and lock-nut and the apparent scarcity of bides. As far as I have been able to ascertain, the experience of Tanners has varied very much. In some cases I hear of considerable pront and lin others of loss. On the whole, howevor, I judge that 11897 will generally be looked back upon as a year of much uncertainty and anxiety." BUILDING."—The Building and Trades have been very busy during the whole of 1897, and the wea- ther being on the whole favourable, there has been no lack of employment. So far ,as I am able to judge, there has been practically no unemployed in any branch of this large and important industry, and the prospects of 1898 are quite as satisfactery." _

From these opinions, then, I should say that 1897 has run its course somewhat uneventfully to the public generally, the bulk of labourers having been steadily employed ; it has not been a year of great fortunes to individuals,but the inhabitants of Warrington have had their full share of the moderate state of prosperity exist- ing generally. POPITLAI lON AND GROWTH OF VTR TOWN. In the absence of a quinquennial census it is nearly Impossible to arrive at a true estimate of the popula- tion, especially with the recent new addition to the borough boundary, but still by Ablating this usual method with the old portion of the town, and '1 elmilar plan with the new, nay eitim'ate for the year 1897 will be safely within the mark. Estimated population mid- summer, 1897 :—Old portion of borough, 59.112; menv extension (taking effect Ist. November, 1899), 2,588 ; total, 61,700. BIRIMS, MARRIAGES AND DEATHS. The number of marriages registered in the borough in the year 1897 was 691, against 514 in 1896, and 450 in 1895. The births registered in the borough during the year 1897, amounted to 1,070 males and 1,199 females, giving a total of 2,269,against 2,143 in the previous year, producing a birth-rate of 36.7 per 1,000 of the notinla- tion. The average birth-rate for the 10 years 1887-96 was 39 1 per 1,000. The excess of births over deaths was 1,025. There is a steady decline in the birth-rate, and this is not confined to the borough of Warrington, but is more or less general throughout the kingdom. The total number of deaths recorded in the borough of Warrington during the year 1897 was 1.244, of which 646 were males, and 598 females. Of the total in 1897, 145 occurred in public institutions, viz s--10 in the fever hospital, 30 in the infirmary, and 105 in the work- house. Of the rite! deaths 37 occurred among persons belonging to outside districts, whilst two deaths occur- red outside the district belonging thereto. In estimating the death-rate these have to be severally deducted from and added to the total. After making the above allow- ances, the number of which the morality for the year is estimated would be 1,209. This is equivalent to a death- rate of 195 per 1,000 ner annum, against a death-rate of 2813 in 1896, 215 in 1895, and 174 in 1894. The average for the 10 years 1887-1896 is 2111. The rate of infantile mortality is higher than in 1898, being 175 per 1,000 births, as compared with 183 in that year. This is 10 above the average in the 10 preceding years. ostt •tf every 1,000 porn, 398 died in their first year, against 351 in 1896, 419 in 1895, and 277 in 1894'. The following table gives the cauaes of infantile mor- tality :—Scarlet fever, nil; measles, 9; whooping cough, 13; diarrisce a, 64; croup 1; tubercular diseases, 15;; brain diseases, including convulsions, 47; lung diseases, 68 ; dentition and diseases of stomach, 42; diseases of skin, ear, &c., 4; prernature birth, 36; debility, 49 ; ill-defined and causes not specified, 48; other diseases, 4.• total 398. The infantile mortality of England and Wales in 1897 was 168 per 1,000 births registered, which was eight per I 1,000 above the average.

TEE SEVEN ZYMOTIC DISEASES. The rate of mortality fremithe ii.ven chief zymotio dis- eases :—Smallpox, nil ; measles 52 ; scarlet fever, 3 ; diphtheria, 3 ; whooping cough, 28 ; fevers. 1; diarr- !ices, 88 ; was 28 per 1,000, being 02 less than in 1898, and above 2 ner 1,000 less than in 1895. The average for the 10 years Preceding 18874898 was 42. The SAMS death-rate in England and Wales was 215 per 1,000 liv- ing, against 217 and 2.21 respectively in the two pre- ceding years. Information on the compulsory netifieation of infecti- ous disease, smallpox vaccination, scarlet fever, diarrhcea, measles, diphtheria, whooping cough a,:d enteric fever is given, with tabulated atatements with regard to the outbreaks of fever in 1897, AMA the report then proceeds, LOCAL DISEASES. Bronchitis and inflammation of the lunge accounted for no le ge than 251 deaths, against 208 in 1898'. Of this number 123 wore under five years of age. The greater fatality from these disease. arose from the prevalence all the year of influenza, which has the power of originat- ing them maladies. From diseases of the heart the deaths numbered 57. Seventy-three deaths *ere referred to diseases of the stomach and bowels, whilst nine and 24 were ascribed te liv-r and kidney disease respec- tively. From the various diseases of the brain and nerv- ous system 129 deaths were registered. This number iucludes 40 from ennvulsions,37 of which were under 5 years, of age. • Malignant disease, or, in oth.r words, cancer, was the cause of 41 deaths, against 32 in 1898. Alcoholism Oaly six deaths were directly attributed te aleoholism, though no doubt many diseases had their -origin in this dangerous article of diet. Violence : The deaths from violence numbered 28. 111-defined causes : Not counting deaths from debility, atrophy. Stc., there were 73 deaths ill-dafined or not specified. Seventy-four were not specified either be medical practitioners or coroner., or nearly 6 per cent. Coroner's inquests were held in 33 Cases. THE SANITARY COND/T/OM OF THIS EAVES MERSEY

-- ADJOltqffl IVILDMRSPOOE-ROLD. In the menth of June it became my duty to make a special refvence to the terribly insanitary condition of this part of the old bed of the river, which for five years has bean practically a huge staynant cesspool of half to two-thirds of a mile in l.mgtis, giving off, under certain climatic conditions.most sickening and offensive odours. Besides the deposit of filth in the bed of the river, which is the filth uf ages, this portion of the river received the sewage of Stockton Heath, the sewage of Wilderspool Brewery in all- stages of temperature and decemp,sition. the boat drainage from 36 houses in Greenall's-avenue (a new portion of the borough) and the local drainage from about 63 houses on the Wilder- speol-road. !tie satisfactory to note that the Paving and Sewerage Committee have constructed a sewer which reemives all the above sewage. and / am now able to report that the borough of Warrington has ceased to be guilty of peuring any portion of its sewage into this part of the river. But there will still remain to be &sit with the accumulated sludge on the old river bed, and I must strongly urge you to take such steps that will pre- vent the racurrpnce of any nuisance.

TUB CHIEF sawirsar REQUISSMINTS. Soc., further hospital pro- vision for the reception of infectious diseases, and the increase of the inspectorial staff.

A BOY KILLED AT A WARRINGTON.
WO RKS.
THE JURY BLAME MASTER AND FOREMAN.

Mr. S. Brighouse county coroner, conducted an en- quiry at the Warrington Police Station, on Monday morning, relative to the death of Thomas Jeffs, aged 14, who was killed by being caught in some shafting at Messrs. Edelstea's Pin Works, Snutsford-road,on Thurs- day.

Mr. J. H. Rogers, factory inspector, and Mr. J. A. Edelsten were present, but at the opening of the in- quest neither had arrived. The Coroner noticed that Messrs. Edelsten were not represented,and asked if they had been sum/toned. Inspector Cox said he had warned them.
The Coroner : They have no plans for me or the jell. I shall adjourn the inquiry. They ought to oe here. Was Mr. Ede!sten warned as a witness ?
Inspector Cox) Yes, sir.

Albert Jeffs, 11, Yorim-st.,father of the deceased boy, said his son was apprenticed to Messrs. Edelsten and Sons about twelve months ago. Witness saw him go to his work on Thursday morning, and later in the morn- ing his wife came and told him of the accident. They proceeded to the Infirmary together, and witness re- mained with the boy till his death. Ail he was able to say was " the shafting." Mr. Edelsten made his appearance at this stage and was asked by the Coroner if he had a plan of the scene of the accident. _
Mr. Edelsten replied in the negative. He said he very easily could have brought one it he had thought one was necessary. _ .

The Corone-r : In the case of accidents in works I thought everyone knew that a plan showing the locus in quo was necessary. The jury very kindly, at my sug- gestion, went and made an inspection of the plies. I thought that would help them, but outside that I am supposed to have on the table a plan showing the place where the accident happened. Mr. Edelsten : I could soon sketch one. Henry Houlding,94 Winwick-road, foreman of the tool department at Messrs. Edelsten's Works,said that in the place where the accident happened there was a shaft making about 150 revolutions a minute, and which was about 9ft. from the ground. There was a beam running parallel with it and the distance between the two was about 5 feet 6 inches. The accident happened on Thurs- day morning,about 10.45. He was sittiag on the beam along which they were going to put a new shaft. Be- tween the shaft and the beam, a ladder was fixed against a cross beam. The deceased moun:ed this ladder and witness handed him a piece of string and told him to put the end of it to the shaft and hold it there while he measured the distance to the place where the new shaft had to be fixed. The ladder was about three feet from the shaft. The deceased went up the ladder with the string in his left haud,and put it to the shaft. Witness then told him to go down and take the ladder to the other end of the shaft. At the same moment he (wit- ness) turned round to go to the other end of the shaft. Ile heard the noise ef the ladder falling to the floor, and on looking round be saw the lad being whirled round the shaft. He could not say how the lad was caught. He did not slip while be had the string in his hand. The shaft was about 4ft. from the roof. The Coroner: Wasn't it rather a dangerous occupation to send a lad up there to put a piece of string close to a shaft that was revolving at the rate of 150 revolutions a minute P—There was no danger attached to it. What had he on—a slop ?—Yee, .a whits slop. . Is that the sort of ladder (the latter was produced) you would expect anyone to go up within 15 inches of a revolving shaft P—lt is all right for a lad. Did you go up yourself P—Yes.
Thera area nimiher of wooden save, iron staves, and pieces of wood nailed across. It is a composite ladder, isn't it ? It looks more like a ladder for the marine stores than for the works.
Witness said the deceased was taken to the Infirmary. He (witnees) could not give any information as to how the accident happened. _ _
tt The Factory Inspector : You say the boy had done his work at that end of the shaft P—Witness : yes. _ _
The Inspector: Did he turn round when he went down the ladder P—lle stood with his bLick to the ladder. The Coroner ; That Beem9 to me a very stupid posi- tion.

In answer to further queries by the Iftspector,witnesa said that the deceased wag not up the ladder two minutes. The shaft was about (ift distant from the beam witness was sitting on. The ladder was about 3ft from the beam. He (witness) had fixed other shafts, but the deceased had not been engaged in such work previously. The shaft was a perfectly smooth one. He did not think the ladder was broken by the weight of the bay. Wit. nese did not take the boy from the shafting, he fell off. Mr. Eletsten told witness to put the new shaft up, and he selected the deceased boy because he was the nearest. The boy oiled the same shaft twins a week, but that was when it was stationary. In reply to a juror, witness thought it probable that one of the iron staves might have given way, and that the deceased had caught hold of the shaft to save himself from falling. The Factory Inspector said there was an impression that smooth revolving shafta were not dangerous, but they were the most dangerous of machinery. There had been hale ndnpn fatal accidents in hie district alone trom machinery of that kind in one year. Mr. J. A. Edelsten, sole proprietor of the works, said he was present when the accident happened. He entered the works about two minutes before and saw the ladder. A moment later he looked up again and saw something spinning round the shalt which looked like a buadle of clothes. Tnen the ladder fell, and the boy fell next. The Coroner : How long has the ladder been in use at your works ? Mr.Edlesten : It is an old ladder. My works are old works. This is a relic which ought to have been chopped Up long ago. The Coroner : What do you think with respect to your foreman's action in putting the lad within two feet of the shafting ? Mr. Edelsten : I should have thought there was not the slightest danger. I have been up since in exactly the same position as the boy, and I did not see any danger. The Coroner : This lad was only 14. Mr. Edelsten : I should not have thought it possible if it bad not happened. Continuins,,,,witness said it was the fall that smashed the ladder. He distinctly saw it. It tell against some machinery and knocked ofrthe top part. Apparently it was thrown over by the boy catch- ing it. Asked by a juror if he thought he ought not to have had the old ladders replaced by better ones,witness said he would see to all the ladders in the future. He was Conethntly attending to such things. The Inspector : Frein my point of view. I would like to emphasize the great danger of approaching revolving shafts. It is the most dangerous part of the machinery we have. I have endeavoured as far as Ii could to show that this accident was due to this dangerous practice of approaching the shaft, not particularly to the ladder going over. I have not yet been able to make a close. Inquiry into the accident, but have certainly formed, that opinion. The accident may have,happened,,and no doubt did happen, when the lad was on the ladder .and would have happened if the ladder had been a goodone.. It is well that manufacturers should knew thatit is very dangerous to approach a revolving shaft, whether there Le any protection on it or not. The Caroner,in sunamiag up, said no one would, gain- say the fact that it was a dangerous practice to ap- proach revolving shafts. It seemed to him that the foreman had put the lad in a place•of danger,, and him- self in a place of safety, and did not supply him. with the appliances to preserve him as much as possible from danger. Mr. Eieleten had candidly admitted that the ladder ought to have been chopped up long, agoband the foreman not only called upon the bey to take up a posi- tion of danger but allowed him to use a rotten old lad- der. If the jury thought that the foreman was neeligent and that the foreman had not provided the necessaay appliances for this kind of work, they were entitled to add that to their verdict. After about ten minutes deliberation in private, the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."' They added that they agreed with the lespectcr that it was dangerous to approach revolving shafting,, and they found that the master and foreman were to blame for allowing an imperfect and rotten ladder to be used for the purpose for which it WAR used, and, they also consi- dered the foreman to blame for allowing a.yoiath to as- sist him in this dangerous work,. The Coroner : Is the foreman here-?

Inspector Cox : No Sir, he has gone. The Coroner H ought not to have been allowed to go It is a piece of impertinence. Eke said be should have told the foreman, if he had been present, that he agreed with the inspector that it was dangerous to ap- proach a revolving shaft, and that it would have been quite easy for him to have taken the measurements when the shaft was at a standstill, when there would have been no danger. Instead of that he had taken "measurements with a shaft revolving at 150 revolutions a minute, and, ladder or no ladder, the action itself was Illegal and wrong. He ought to have waited until the shaft was stopped; at dinner time or slum other time. If it was absolutely necessary for him to take these measurements whilst the shaft was revolving he ought ta have placed himself in danger rather than a youth of 14, and he ought to have used the best appliances poss- ible and not the ladder they had seen.
